It is Windows-only by design until the whole system works, it ships no release yet, and it has no test suite by owner directive — every claim below is verified by hand against real bytes on disk. Live project state lives **only** in [GitHub issues](https://github.com/ChrisRoyse/Astrolabe/issues); this README is the story, [EPIC #65](https://github.com/ChrisRoyse/Astrolabe/issues/65) is the truth.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 1 — A navigator with no stars\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/01-problem.jpg\" alt=\"An AI agent adrift on a sea of text with no stars to steer by\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nEvery AI coding agent today works from **text**. It greps. It reads a file. It infers structure from whatever it happened to open. Its context is a sample, its confidence is uncalibrated, and it has no memory of what was true last week or what actually broke last time.\n\nEven the best open-source code-graph servers — and [codebase-memory-mcp](cbm/) is the best decomposer in the open-source world — stop at the graph. They know *that* `f` calls `g`. They do not know whether that fact ever **mattered**: whether a test ever failed because of it, whether an incident ever traced through it, whether an agent's last change there was reverted. Their weights are hand-set constants, identical for a Haskell compiler and a React storefront. Their thresholds are fixed. Nothing is grounded, nothing is validated, and the system is exactly as smart on day 400 as on day 1.\n\nAn agent steering by that graph is a navigator with a map and no stars.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 2 — Two halves of one instrument\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/02-two-halves.jpg\" alt=\"codebase-memory-mcp and Calyx as two halves of one astrolabe\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nASTROLABE begins with an observation: two mature codebases, written independently, are each the missing half of the other.\n\n| | **codebase-memory-mcp** (`cbm/`) | **Calyx** (`calyx/`) |\n|---|---|---|\n| Language | C — ~120K lines of engine source, single static binary | Rust — ~557K lines across 24 crates |\n| What it does | **Decomposes** a repository into atoms and **associates** them: tree-sitter across **158 languages**, a hybrid type-aware LSP reverse-engineered from nine real language servers, **40+ typed edge types** (`CALLS`, `DATA_FLOWS`, `TESTS`, `HTTP_CALLS`, `EMITS`, `CROSS_*`, …), git context, watcher, incremental indexing, a 14-tool MCP surface | An **association-native database and grounded-intelligence engine**: an LSM vault with MVCC time-travel, cross-terms and reactive triggers, mutual-information measurement in bits, kernel distillation, a per-slot conformal guard, a prediction oracle, a hash-chained provenance ledger, and a reversible self-optimizer |\n| What it lacks | An intelligence layer: every weight guessed, nothing grounded, nothing improves | A code-domain front end: no parser, no graph extractor, no agent surface |\n\nNeither needed to be rewritten. Both were pulled into this repository **once**, and are now owned, first-class ASTROLABE source — edited directly, evolved in place. There are no pins, no patch overlays, no upstream tracking. The origin repos are, at most, a quarry.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 3 — The method\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/03-method.jpg\" alt=\"Decompose, Associate, Differentiate, Compose\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nCalyx's builder's handbook ([`docs/BUILDING_ON_CALYX.md`](docs/BUILDING_ON_CALYX.md)) has one foundational rule: *atoms → all base associations → differentiate → kernel → compose; never shortcut it.* CBM already performs the first two steps for the code domain more completely than any hand-built ingestion pipeline in any domain. Calyx is the engine for the last two.\n\n```\ncodebase-memory-mcp                          Calyx\n──────────────────────                       ─────────────────────────\n① DECOMPOSE  158-lang tree-sitter      →     measure: every symbol becomes a\n             + hybrid LSP → symbols          constellation through a lens panel\n② ASSOCIATE  40+ edge types,           →     count: cross-terms, agreement graph\n             cross-service, cross-repo,      ③ DIFFERENTIATE  bits, sufficiency,\n             git co-change, similarity          redundancy, synergy, causality\n                                             ④ COMPOSE  kernel, guard, oracle,\n                                                ledger, anneal, fused search\n```\n\n> **The thesis in one line:** CBM turns a repository into atoms and associations. Calyx turns atoms and associations into intelligence. Wire the output of the first into the input of the second, ground the result in real developer outcomes, and the loop closes — an MCP that gets measurably smarter about *your* codebase every day it is used.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 4 — Every symbol becomes a constellation\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/04-constellation.jpg\" alt=\"A code symbol measured through a ring of 24 lenses\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nThe astrolabe is the instrument for navigating by constellations. In ASTROLABE, the atomic record *is* a constellation: every function, class, struct, route, channel and module that CBM extracts is measured through a **panel of ~24 frozen lenses** (`S0`–`S22`) built almost entirely from signals CBM already computes — AST profiles, complexity, MinHash structure, API/type/decorator signatures, error surfaces, git temporal data, graph position — plus a small set of learned embeddings kept strictly separate from the deterministic encoders.\n\nTwo identities hold it all together ([`crates/astrolabe-domain`](crates/astrolabe-domain)):\n\n- a **series identity** — the qualified name, stable across versions, and\n- a **version identity** (`CxId`) — the content address of *(project, qualified name, canonical source bytes)*, so the same code always yields the same id and a changed byte always yields a new one.\n\nLens contracts are **frozen**: a lens that changes its shape is a new lens, never a silent edit, so measurements remain comparable across months of history. Anything that tries to violate that is refused with `CALYX_LENS_FROZEN_VIOLATION`.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 5 — Grounding\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/05-anchors.jpg\" alt=\"Constellations anchored to the seabed by tests, CI runs, traces, git history and agent outcomes\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nA graph without outcomes is opinion. ASTROLABE attaches **anchors** — real-world outcomes — to real symbols:\n\n| Anchor source | Tool | Trust |\n|---|---|---|\n| Test-suite reports (`junit_xml`, `cargo_test_json`, `pytest_verbose`, `go_test_json`, `vitest_json`) | `anchor_outcome` | `ci:` sources are **Trusted** (confidence exactly 1.0) |\n| Coverage reports (`lcov`, `coverage_py_json`, `cobertura_xml`) mapped line-exact to symbols | `coverage_ingest` | resolved, 1.0; one-hop `TESTS` propagation is proxy, 0.6 |\n| Runtime traces (OTLP protobuf / JSON) — production calls promote matching edges to Trusted and flag 5xx incidents | `ingest_traces` | Trusted |\n| Git archaeology — SZZ bug-introducing commits, reverts, fix commits | automatic on shadow index | `git:revert:` Trusted; `git:fix:` Provisional |\n| AI-agent task outcomes — the flywheel's own feedback | `anchor_outcome` with `agent:` | Provisional |\n\nThe trust of an anchor is decided by its source prefix and is **not negotiable**. Every anchor is written to the ledger, and every erasure (`anchor_erase`) is a tombstone plus a ledger entry — append-only physically, destructive to the serving view.\n\nThis is the difference between \"these two functions look related\" and \"these two functions have actually broken together before.\"\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 6 — Assay: bits, not guesses\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/06-assay.jpg\" alt=\"A balance scale weighing guessed constants against measured bits\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nCBM's original intelligence layer had an 11-signal semantic score with hand-set weights, fixed thresholds at 0.75 and 0.95, and edge confidences pinned at 0.5 / 0.55 / 0.75 / 0.90 / 0.95 — none measured against anything real, two of the eleven signals dead code.\n\nASTROLABE's **Assay** ([`crates/astrolabe-assay`](crates/astrolabe-assay), on Calyx's KSG mutual-information estimators) replaces every one of those with a per-repository **measurement in bits**, exposed through `measure_bits`:\n\n- `signals` — bits per lens slot about a real outcome axis, with confidence intervals\n- `sufficiency` — *I(panel; axis)* against *H(axis)*: literally \"how much of this outcome can our measurements explain, and what is missing\"\n- `redundancy` — total correlation, effective rank, pairwise map\n- `synergy` — three-way interaction information\n- `causality` — transfer-entropy `DRIVES` edges with lag sweep\n- `calibration` — each edge-resolution strategy's measured precision versus its prior, with Wilson intervals\n\n`assay_gate` then admits, parks or retires candidate lenses from those cards — ledgered and **reversible** byte-for-byte. The standing invariant behind all of it: **no constant that could be a measurement.**\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 7 — The Kernel\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/07-kernel.jpg\" alt=\"A galaxy of symbols with a small blazing core — the kernel\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nMost of a codebase is explained by a small part of it. The **kernel** ([`crates/astrolabe-kernel`](crates/astrolabe-kernel)) is that part, found rather than guessed: a deterministic full-graph feedback-vertex-set selection with a residual-DAG proof, a complete member index, and a **recall gate** — the kernel must meet an explicitly declared recall threshold (the blueprint's target is ≥ 0.95) against a corpus of real external queries before it is allowed to serve. The threshold is a required admission parameter, not a hidden constant.\n\n- `get_kernel` — build, read, and audit one atomically selected kernel generation; grounding-gap reports name the unanchored regions\n- `kernel_answer` — grounded Q&A: resolve an anchored entry point, walk association edges outward with `hop_score = edge_weight × 0.9^hop`, every hop carrying its ledger reference; refuse with a per-lens deficit rather than answer ungrounded\n\nThe kernel is the context engine. The flagship product built on it — a token-budgeted, recall-gated, reproducible **context pack** — is the one big piece still ahead (Chapter 16).\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 8 — The Guard\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/08-guard.jpg\" alt=\"A lighthouse sorting incoming code into accept, new region, quarantine and refuse\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nBefore agent-written code lands, the **Guard** ([`crates/astrolabe-guard`](crates/astrolabe-guard), on Calyx's conformal Ward) asks one question: *does this look like the code that works here?*\n\nIt measures the candidate on **the same instruments as indexing**, compares it per-slot against kernel-near trusted exemplars (`code_semantic`, `struct_trigrams`, `api_callees`, `name_semantic`, `complexity_profile`, `error_surface`, `public_api_signature`), and combines the per-slot verdicts — never a flattened average — into **`accept` / `new_region` / `quarantine` / `refuse`**, at a calibrated false-accept rate.\n\nThe calibration corpus builds itself: `guard_calibrate mode:\"generated\"` mutates real HEAD source, mines revert records, and borrows alien constellations from other indexed projects, enforcing a mix policy (≥ 50 bad cases, ≥ 3 generators, ≤ 60 % per generator) and failing closed on an under-mixed corpus. No hand-labelled data.\n\n`guard_lock` identity-locks a public API so breaking changes to it refuse; `guard_commit_ood` scores a whole commit; `guard_advisory_hook` is the 300 ms never-blocking fast path for editor hooks.\n\n> What the guard is not: it measures *distributional conformance to trusted exemplars*. It tells you \"this does not look like the code that works here.\" It does not tell you the code is correct — that is what the verification loop (Chapter 12) is for.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 9 — The Oracle\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/09-oracle.jpg\" alt=\"A compass rose with consequences rippling outward from one changed symbol\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nCBM's old `detect_changes` mapped hop-distance to risk: one hop away meant CRITICAL. That is topology, not evidence. The **Oracle** ([`crates/astrolabe-oracle`](crates/astrolabe-oracle)) grounds prediction in observed change→outcome history:\n\n| Question | Tool | How it answers |\n|---|---|---|\n| *If I change X, what breaks?* | `predict_impact` | cycle-guarded butterfly walk over real edges (×0.7 per hop, prune < 0.05, depth ≤ 4), three independent ceilings keeping probability strictly below 1.0; consequences crossing `TESTS` edges become a **ranked test-selection set** |\n| *This failed — what most plausibly caused it?* | `abduce_cause` | the same walk backwards; structural-only candidates capped at 0.35 and labelled provisional; every hypothesis names its **disconfirming test** |\n| *When will this flaky test bite again?* | `forecast` | median inter-arrival, credible interval, overdue hazard, CUSUM regime changes; refuses on self-inconsistent evidence |\n| *Is the system ready for questions about this scope?* | `get_readiness` | a six-tier predicate that fails closed per tier |\n| *What are the identifiable causal effects here?* | `causal_analysis`, `expected_gain` | persisted identifiable effects and expected net gains |\n\nAnd the honesty gate over all of it: a question the panel cannot support is **refused with a deficit**, never answered with a confident guess.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 10 — Provenance\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/... [L2]   "content": "# Living AI Agent System\n\n![Living AI Ecosystem](screenshot.png)\n\nA browser-based visualization of AI agents moving in a dynamic ecosystem, creating flowing patterns and trails. Built with **Three.js** and **TypeScript**, this project brings AI agents to life in a mesmerizing 3D environment, where they interact and evolve in real-time. Each agent follows a leader, forming a chain of movement with oscillating trails, all rendered directly in your browser using WebGL.\n\n---\n\n## Features\n\n- **Real-time 3D Visualization**: Watch AI agents move and interact in a flowing, dynamic pattern.\n- **Agent Behavior**: Agents follow a leader in a chain, creating a snake-like movement with oscillating trails.\n- **Unique Visuals**: Each agent has a distinct color and leaves a fading trail, adding depth and beauty to the scene.\n- **Screen Wrapping**: Agents seamlessly reappear on the opposite side when they move off-screen, creating a continuous environment.\n- **Tech Stack**:\n  - **Three.js**: For WebGL rendering, enabling smooth and performant 3D graphics in the browser.\n  - **TypeScript**: For type safety and better development experience.\n  - **Vite**: For fast development and building, providing instant feedback during development.\n\n---\n\n## Installation\n\nTo get started with the Living AI Agent System, follow these steps:\n\n### Prerequisites\n\nEnsure you have the following installed:\n- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) (version 14 or higher recommended)\n- [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) (comes with Node.js)\n\n### Steps\n\n1. **Clone the Repository**:\n   ```bash\n   git clone https://github.com/yourusername/livingai.git\n   ```\n   *Replace `yourusername` with your actual GitHub username.*\n\n2. **Navigate to the Project Directory**:\n   ```bash\n   cd livingai\n   ```\n\n3. **Install Dependencies**:\n   ```bash\n   npm install\n   ```\n   This will install all required packages, including Three.js, TypeScript, and Vite, as specified in `package.json`.\n\n---\n\n## Usage\n\nOnce installed, you can run the project in various modes:\n\n### Development Mode\n\nStart the development server to view the visualization in real-time:\n```bash\nnpm run dev\n```\n- This launches a server at `http://localhost:6873`.\n- The page updates automatically as you make changes to the code, thanks to Vite's hot module replacement.\n\n### Build for Production\n\nCreate an optimized production build:\n```bash\nnpm run build\n```\n- This compiles the TypeScript code and bundles the assets into the `dist` folder.\n- The build is optimized for performance and ready for deployment.\n\n### Preview the Build\n\nServe the production build locally to test it:\n```bash\nnpm run preview\n```\n- This starts a local server to preview the contents of the `dist` folder.\n\n---\n\n## How It Works\n\nThe Living AI Agent System simulates a chain of AI agents, each following the one before it, creating a flowing, organic movement. The agents are rendered as colored spheres with trails that fade over time, adding a sense of motion and depth to the visualization.\n\n### Scene Setup\n\n- The scene is initialized using Three.js, with a black background (`0x000000`) for contrast.\n- A perspective camera is used, positioned at `z = 30` to provide a clear view of the agents.\n- The WebGL renderer is set up with antialiasing for smooth edges and full-screen rendering.\n\n### EcoAgent Class\n\nEach agent is an instance of the `EcoAgent` class, defined in `main.ts`. The class manages the following properties and behaviors:\n\n#### Properties\n\n- **Position** (`THREE.Vector3`): The current location of the agent in 3D space.\n- **Velocity** (`THREE.Vector3`): The direction and speed of movement.\n- **Trail** (`THREE.Vector3[]`): An array of past positions, used to render the agent's trail.\n- **Color** (`THREE.Color`): A unique color for the agent and its trail.\n- **Leader** (`EcoAgent | null`): The agent this instance follows, if any.\n- **Followers** (`EcoAgent[]`): List of agents following this instance.\n- **Phase** (`number`): Used for oscillation in movement, adding natural variation.\n\n#### Constructor\n\n- Initializes the agent with a random starting position and velocity.\n- Assigns a unique color and sets up the trail with the starting position.\n- Randomizes the phase for oscillation effects.\n\n#### Update Method\n\nThe `update` method is called each frame to update the agent's position and behavior:\n\n- **If the Agent Has a Leader (Follower Behavior)**:\n  - Targets a point in the leader's trail (10 steps behind, or the leader's current position if the trail is shorter).\n  - Calculates the direction to the target and normalizes it.\n  - Adds oscillation by computing a perpendicular vector and scaling it with a sine function, creating a wavy, natural motion.\n  - Adjusts speed based on distance to the leader, ensuring smooth following behavior.\n  - Updates velocity using linear interpolation (`lerp`) for gradual changes.\n\n- **If the Agent Is a Leader (No Leader)**:\n  - Moves in a flowing pattern using sine and cosine functions for the x and y directions.\n  - Updates velocity using `lerp` for smooth transitions.\n\n- **Position Update**:\n  - Adds the velocity to the position to move the agent.\n  - Implements screen wrapping:\n    - If the agent moves beyond ±30 units in x or y, it reappears on the opposite side.\n    - This creates a continuous, boundary-less environment.\n\n- **Trail Update**:\n  - Adds the current position to the trail.\n  - Limits the trail to 50 points, removing the oldest point if necessary.\n\n### Agent Chain Setup\n\n- 25 agents are created with random starting positions and colors.\n- The agents are connected in a chain:\n  - The first agent (index 0) is the leader and has no leader.\n  - Each subsequent agent follows the previous one (e.g., agent 1 follows agent 0, agent 2 follows agent 1, etc.).\n  - Leaders store references to their followers, forming a bidirectional chain.\n\n### Rendering\n\n- **Agent Meshes**:\n  - Each agent is represented as a sphere (`THREE.SphereGeometry`, radius 0.2, 16 segments).\n  - Uses `THREE.MeshBasicMaterial` with the agent's unique color.\n  - Added to the scene and updated each frame with the agent's position.\n\n- **Trail Lines**:\n  - Each trail is rendered as a line (`THREE.Line`) using `THREE.BufferGeometry`.\n  - The trail geometry is updated each frame with the agent's trail positions.\n  - Uses `THREE.LineBasicMaterial` with:\n    - The agent's color.\n    - Transparency (`opacity: 0.5`) and additive blending for a glowing, fading effect.\n\n- **Animation Loop**:\n  - Runs continuously using `requestAnimationFrame`.\n  - Updates each agent's position and trail using the `EcoAgent` class.\n  - Updates the corresponding mesh and trail line in the scene.\n  - Renders the scene with the camera using the WebGL renderer.\n\n---\n\n## Configuration\n\nYou can customize the simulation by modifying the following in `main.ts`:\n\n### Number of Agents\n\n- Adjust the loop that creates the agents:\n  ```typescript\n  for (let i = 0; i < 25; i++) {\n  ```\n  - Change `25` to the desired number of agents.\n  - Note: Each agent after the first will follow the previous one, forming a longer or shorter chain.\n\n### Screen Bounds\n\n- Modify the `bounds` variable:\n  ```typescript\n  const bounds = 30;\n  ```\n  - This sets the wrapping area to ±30 units in x and y.\n  - Increase or decrease this value to change the size of the visible area.\n\n### Other Potential Adjustments\n\n- **Agent Size**: Modify the sphere geometry in the rendering section (e.g., change the radius from 0.2).\n- **Trail Length**: Adjust the trail limit in the `update` method (e.g., change `50` to a different number).\n- **Movement Speed**: Adjust the speed factors in the `update` method (e.g., `speed = THREE.MathUtils.clamp(distance * 0.1, 0.05, 0.2)`).\n- **Oscillation Amplitude/Frequency**: Modify the oscillation parameters in the follower behavior (e.g., change `Math.sin(time * 0.002 + this.phase) * 0.5`).\n\n---\n\n## Project Structure\n\nThe project is organized as follows:\n\n- **`src/main.ts`**: Core logic, including the `EcoAgent` class, scene setup, and animation loop.\n- **`src/style.css`**: Minimal CSS for full-screen rendering:\n  - Resets margins and padding.\n  - Hides overflow to ensure the visualization fills the screen.\n- **`index.html`**: Basic HTML structure linking the CSS and TypeScript files.\n- **`vite-env.d.ts`**: Type definitions for Vite environment variables (currently unused).\n- **`vite.config.ts`**: Vite configuration, specifying the development server port (6873) and build target (`esnext`).\n- **`tsconfig.json`**: TypeScript configuration, enabling strict type checking and ESNext modules.\n- **`package.json`**: Project metadata, scripts, and dependencies.\n\n---\n\n## Dependencies\n\nThe project uses the following dependencies (listed in `package.json`):\n\n### Runtime Dependencies\n\n- **`three`**: For 3D rendering with WebGL.\n- **`typescript`**: For type-safe development.\n- **`@types/node`**: Type definitions for Node.js (used by TypeScript).\n- **`dspy.ts`**: Not currently used in the provided code; possibly for future AI integration.\n- **`onnxruntime-web`**: Not currently used; possibly for future machine learning model execution.\n\n### Development Dependencies\n\n- **`@types/three`**: Type definitions for Three.js.\n- **`vite`**: Fast build tool and development server.\n\nNote: Dependencies like `dspy.ts` and `onnxruntime-web` are not used in the current implementation. is a database whose native record is the *association-constellation*: one input measured through many frozen embedders (\"lenses\"), fused, differentiated by the information each one adds, and It finds the small grounding **kernel** that explains a whole dataset, **guards** generated content against drift and out-of-distribution answers, keeps a tamper-evident **ledger** of how every answer was produced, and gets faster the more you use it.\n\nA *calyx* is the whorl of sepals that holds a flower together at its base — the grounded structure from which a constellation of petals opens. That is exactly what this database is: a grounded base (kernel + provenance) that holds a constellation of vectors and lets it bloom into search, naming, and answers.\n\n---\n\n## 🧩 Calyx is a base, not a finished product\n\n**Calyx is a template.** It computes associations — it measures one input through many lenses, fuses them, finds the grounding kernel, guards every answer, and records provenance. But the moment an association *means* something specific — something you can infer, recognize, or act on — that recognition-and-trigger logic is code *you* write for *your* data. Every Calyx database holds different data, forms different associations, and unlocks different meanings; what happens the instant a meaning is recognized is custom to each project.\n\nThat is by design, and it is why Calyx will always be a **base** rather than a shrink-wrapped product. You don't ship the template — you refactor it into your specific use case, exactly like starting a product from a frontend template instead of a blank page. Beginning from the Calyx base, you are already *very* far along: the hard, reusable machinery (constellations, kernel, guard, ledger) is built and grounded for you. What remains is the part only you can write — the meaning your data unlocks, and what your system does when it sees it.\n\n---\n\n## ✨ Why Calyx\n\nEvery time you build a serious retrieval or intelligence system, you end up gluing the same machinery together by hand: a vector store for semantics, a keyword index for lexical match, a graph database for relationships, a pile of bespoke code to combine embedders, more code to measure whether a new embedder actually helps, and *still* nothing that tells you when your AI's answer has wandered outside what your data can support.\n\nCalyx bakes that machinery **once, into the storage engine**.\n\n<div align=\"center\">\n<img src=\"assets/vs-oldway.jpg\" alt=\"A tangle of disconnected databases and glue code, versus one unified Calyx constellation\" width=\"90%\" />\n</div>\n\n| What a multi-signal system needs | Vector DB / pgvector / Elastic / Neo4j | **Calyx bakes in** |\n|---|---|---|\n| Many embedders, each versioned & frozen | You build the lifecycle yourself | **Registry** — add/retire lenses; prunes redundant ones |\n| Relationships between records | A separate graph database | **Loom** + **Lodestar** — associations are native; the explanatory *kernel* is discoverable |\n| Stop the AI from answering off-distribution | Nothing | **Ward** — a calibrated, fail-closed guard on every answer |\n| Prove how an answer was produced | Metadata columns, best effort | **Ledger** — hash-chained, tamper-evident provenance |\n| Get faster with use | Manual index / quantization tuning | **Anneal** — safe, reversible self-optimization |\n\n> [!NOTE]\n> A vector database is a **one-lens Calyx**: a single embedder plus nearest-neighbor search. Calyx is built for the case where one signal is never enough.\n\n---\n\n## 🌟 The core idea: constellations\n\nA traditional database stores a **row**. A vector database stores a **point**. Calyx stores a **constellation**: one input, measured through many independent *lenses* (embedders and feature extractors), each producing its own typed slot-vector — kept **separate**, never flattened into one opaque blob.\n\n<div align=\"center\">\n<img src=\"assets/constellation-model.jpg\" alt=\"One input passes through seven lenses, each producing a cluster of vectors that fuse into one constellation with a gold kernel at its center\" width=\"95%\" />\n</div>\n\nCalyx is organized around four verbs — the calculus of association:\n\n| Verb | What it means | Subsystem |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Measure** | Assemble a constellation by viewing one input through every lens in a panel | Registry, Aster |\n| **Count** | Derive the associations *between* slots (agreement, delta, interaction) | Loom |\n| **Differentiate** | Quantify the unique information each lens contributes about real outcomes | Assay |\n| **Compose** | Find the explanatory kernel, guard generation, and answer with provenance | Lodestar, Ward, Ledger |\n\nThree principles make the results trustworthy:\n\n- **Grounding is mandatory.** Every claim is measured against real, anchored outcomes. Ungrounded results are explicitly tagged *provisional* rather than presented as fact.\n- **Keep slots separate (no-flatten).** Signals stay typed and independent end-to-end, so you can always see *which* lens drove a result.\n- **Fail closed.** Unknown lens, shape mismatch, uncalibrated guard, missing data → a structured error, never a silent wrong answer.\n\n---\n\n## 🚀 Build from source\n\n> [!IMPORTANT]\n> Calyx is a Rust workspace (`edition 2024`, toolchain `1.95`). No screen-scraping cloud service, no remote agent,\nno data leaving your PC. Synapse is Windows-native to the metal: Win32 `SendInput`, UI\nAutomation, Windows Graphics Capture / DXGI, optional debug-gated WASAPI audio capture,\nand local process control.\n\n---\n\n## What you can do with it\n\nSynapse exposes **40 focused MCP tools** — a small, clean facade surface where every tool\ntakes an explicit `operation`, and every mutating action names the source of truth it\nreads back from. (One tool, the raw browser debugger, is break-glass–gated behind an\nexplicit profile switch.) Here's what those 40 tools unlock.\n\n### 👁️ It can see — structured perception\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/perception.png\" alt=\"Synapse perceives the screen as structured data\" align=\"right\" width=\"42%\">\n\nSynapse hands the model the screen as **clean, low-token structured data**, not a giant\nscreenshot it has to squint at:\n\n- **`observe`** — the focused window, the full UI Automation element tree (every button,\n  field, and menu with its on-screen box), detected entities, and HUD.\n- **`find`** — locate any element or on-screen entity by name, role, or free text.\n- **`read_text`** — OCR any region or element. Reads pixels directly, so it works even\n  where the accessibility API can't reach (canvases and custom UIs).\n- **`screenshot`** — per-window Windows Graphics Capture (and GIF capture), so an agent\n  can photograph *its own* window even when it's behind yours.\n- **`subscribe`** — stream live events (focus changes, new windows, audio) instead of\n  polling.\n- **Browser DOM mode** — Synapse-launched Chromium browsers expose real page nodes\n  through CDP; `observe` and `find` merge them in.\n\nAll of it is **window-targetable**: point a session at a specific window with\n`target` (`operation=set`) and perception watches *that* window — focused or not.\n\n<br clear=\"all\">\n\n### 🖱️ It can act — precise, human-like control\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/action.png\" alt=\"Synapse moves the mouse, types, and draws\" align=\"left\" width=\"42%\">\n\nReal input, synthesized through Win32 — not brittle macros. Everything routes through the\none **`act`** facade (`operation=invoke`), which picks the right delivery path per verb:\n\n- **click, stroke, scroll** — mouse control with timing profiles for point/element moves,\n  optional-button drags, and explicit shaped paths.\n- **type, press, keymap, combo** — type Unicode text with *human-like* keystroke dynamics,\n  press chords, or fire profile-defined key aliases.\n- **set_value** — set a field's value directly through UI Automation and read it back from\n  the source of truth — no keystrokes needed.\n- **clipboard, launch, focus** — clipboard round-trips, launching apps (including *hidden*\n  launches that never flash a window), and explicit, lease-gated window focus via\n  `act operation=foreground`.\n\nActions don't just *fire* — they **verify**. Every click, keystroke, and value write is\nread back from a separate source of truth (UIA state, CDP DOM, even OCR of the pixels) so\nthe agent knows the action *actually landed*, not just that the input was sent.\n\n<br clear=\"all\">\n\n### 🎯 It moves like a human — wind-mouse motion\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/humanized-motion.png\" alt=\"Humanized wind-mouse motion versus robotic linear movement\" align=\"right\" width=\"42%\">\n\nRobotic, perfectly-straight cursor teleports are a tell — and some UIs (canvases,\ndrag-and-drop) outright break on them. The `act` stroke path generates **physically\nplausible motion**: a **wind-mouse model** with gravity and turbulence so every path bends\nand wavers like a real hand, **velocity profiles** that accelerate out and decelerate in\nalong the *curve*, and **explicit shaped paths** to draw a star, trace a signature, or drag\na slider along an exact polyline. Every stroke is audited with its motion model and path ID.\n\n<br clear=\"all\">\n\n### 🌐 It can browse — silent background web control\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/browser-control.png\" alt=\"Synapse drives browser tabs as structured DOM data, silently, in the background\" align=\"left\" width=\"42%\">\n\nThe web isn't pixels to Synapse — it's **structured DOM data**, and it can work it\n*without ever touching your mouse or stealing a tab*:\n\n- **`browser_tabs`** — open, select, and close **background tabs** that never become the\n  active tab. The page you're reading stays exactly where it is.\n- **`browser_nav`** — navigate, reload, back, and forward, all in the background.\n- **`browser_dom`** — read page content, locate and inspect nodes, and pull ARIA\n  snapshots straight from the DevTools accessibility tree.\n- **`browser_form`** — set values and fill forms through CDP (`insertText`, dispatched\n  events) instead of the cursor, so web forms fill while the browser sits behind your work.\n- **`browser_wait` · `browser_capture` · `browser_storage`** — wait on conditions,\n  screenshot pages and read downloads, and read/write cookies and storage.\n- **Graceful fallback ladder** — raw CDP → bundled extension bridge → OCR over the rendered\n  page → honest `uia_only`, with diagnostics that tell the agent *which* path it got.\n\nThis is the engine behind \"message 300 investors\" and \"fill out 270 applications\" — silent,\nbackground, tab-by-tab.\n\n<br clear=\"all\">\n\n### 🔭 It tracks change — delta-first reality\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/delta-reality.png\" alt=\"Delta-first reality streams only what changed\" align=\"right\" width=\"42%\">\n\nRe-sending the whole screen on every step is slow and expensive. The **`reality`** facade\ntakes a **baseline**, then streams the agent **only what changed** — and audits its own\nassumptions against physical reality:\n\n- **`reality operation=baseline`** — a compact, redacted snapshot (~hundreds of tokens).\n- **`reality operation=delta`** — ordered, field-level changes since a cursor. Change a\n  clipboard, a window, a value — you get back *just that delta*.\n- **`reality operation=audit`** — re-reads the real machine and reports drift, forcing a\n  rebase when the agent's mental model has gone stale.\n\nThe payoff: token cost stays flat across a 12-screen wizard or an hours-long run.\n\n<br clear=\"all\">\n\n### 🧭 It learns your routine — mining + proactive assist\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/routine-assist.png\" alt=\"Synapse mines your repetitive workflows and offers to automate them\" align=\"left\" width=\"42%\">\n\nSynapse doesn't just do what it's told — it watches how *you* work and finds the loops\nworth automating:\n\n- **`routine`** — mine repetitive workflows from the activity timeline (`operation=mine`),\n  inspect and label them, take your feedback, and **turn a recognized routine into an armed\n  automation** (`operation=automate`).\n- **`assist`** — read the current intent, detect what you're trying to do, and surface\n  **suggestions** you can accept or dismiss (`operation=suggestion_list` /\n  `suggestion_accept`).\n- **`timeline` · `episode`** — a searchable activity timeline and episodic memory of what\n  happened, so both you and the agent can look back at what worked.\n\nThe result: the boring sequence you do fifteen times a day becomes one \"automate this\" button.\n\n<br clear=\"all\">\n\n### 🤝 It keeps you in the loop — approvals, gates & verification\n\n<img src=\"docs/assets/human-in-loop.png\" alt=\"The agent asks a human for a decision before acting on anything important\" align=\"right\" width=\"42%\">\n\nA tireless agent that acts without asking is a liability. Synapse builds **human-in-the-loop\ncontrol** into the surface itself:\n\n- **`approval`** — the agent can **request approval**, **gate** a sensitive action behind a\n  decision, or **ask the operator** directly — and wait for a yes/no before proceeding.\n- **`escalation`** — configurable escalation rules and an acknowledgement queue, so the\n  agent knows *when* to stop and get a human.\n- **`verification`** — actions are verified against independent sources of truth; the\n  verification inbox and audit let you prove *what actually happened*, not just what was\n  attempted.\n\nSo the overnight agent runs hard on the safe stuff and **pauses to ask** on anything that\nneeds... It now supports **multiple programming languages and frameworks**, creating a comprehensive \"digital twin\" of your entire software ecosystem. This enables unprecedented code comprehension, visualization, and AI-driven development workflows across complex, multi-language projects.\n\n## 🌟 What's New: Multi-Language Support\n\nCodeGraph Analyzer now provides robust support for a wide spectrum of programming languages and frameworks:\n\n### Programming Languages\n- **TypeScript/JavaScript** - Full support for modern TS/JS features with ts-morph\n- **Python** - Complete parsing via Python's native AST module\n- **Java** - Advanced analysis using tree-sitter-java\n- **C#** - Comprehensive parsing with tree-sitter-c-sharp\n- **C/C++** - Detailed analysis of headers, includes, and implementation\n- **Go** - Complete structure and package relationship mapping\n- **SQL** - Table, view, and query analysis from SQL files\n- **HTML/CSS** - Structure and style mapping\n\n### Frameworks & Technologies\n- **React/Preact** - Component hierarchies, JSX elements, prop mapping\n- **Tailwind CSS** - Class usage and relationships\n- **Supabase** - Database schema and API relationships\n- **Deno** - Module, import, and runtime analysis\n\n## 🚀 Key Features\n\n- **Cross-Language Analysis**: Analyze relationships between different languages in the same project\n- **Comprehensive Scanning**: Intelligently identifies supported file types across your entire project\n- **Two-Pass Analysis**: First builds detailed ASTs for each file, then resolves complex cross-file relationships\n- **Rich Element Identification**: Extracts files, directories, classes, interfaces, functions, methods, variables, parameters, type aliases, components, SQL tables, and more\n- **Relationship Mapping**: Maps IMPORTS, EXPORTS, CALLS, EXTENDS, IMPLEMENTS, HAS_METHOD, RENDERS_ELEMENT, USES_COMPONENT, REFERENCES_TABLE, and many others\n- **Neo4j Integration**: Creates a queryable knowledge graph with optimized schema management\n- **MCP Integration**: Works seamlessly with Model Context Protocol for AI-powered codebase interaction\n\n## 🔍 Why Multi-Language Support Matters\n\nModern software development rarely happens in a single language. The expanded language support in CodeGraph Analyzer addresses critical challenges:\n\n- **Unified View**: See your entire tech stack as a coherent system instead of isolated silos\n- **Cross-Language Dependencies**: Trace relationships between frontend and backend components (e.g., React components calling Python APIs)\n- **Microservice Architecture**: Understand service boundaries and communication patterns across different languages\n- **Multi-Team Collaboration**: Enable specialists in different languages to see how their code impacts the broader system\n- **Legacy Integration**: Map connections between newer and older components written in different languages\n- **Complete AI Context**: Give AI assistants holistic understanding of your entire codebase regardless of Understanding\n\nThe true breakthrough of CodeGraph isn't just in what languages it parses, but in how it enables AI to **truly understand your code** through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration with Neo4j.\n\n### How It Works: The Neural Bridge Between Human, AI, and Code\n\n1. **Natural Language → Cypher Translation**: When you ask your AI assistant a question about your understanding the full impact of changes\n\n- **Complexity Navigation**: Handle questions about massive codebases no human could fully keep in their head (\"Show me all places where user data is accessed across our entire stack\")\n\n### Example Queries That Become Possible\n\n```\n\"Show me all React components that fetch data from our Python API endpoints\"\n\n\"Which SQL queries modify the user table and what services call them?\"\n\n\"How does data flow from our frontend form to the database?\"\n\n\"What would break if I changed the return type of this C++ function?\"\n\n\"Generate a [https://github.com/neo4j-contrib/mcp-neo4j](https://github.com/neo4j-contrib/mcp-neo4j)\n\n1. **code-analyzer-mcp**: This MCP server provides AI assistants with the ability to:\n   - Trigger codebase **github.com/neo4j-contrib/mcp-neo4j**: This powerful MCP server is the bridge between natural language and code knowledge, providing:\n   - **read-neo4j-cypher**: Translates natural questions into      \"autoApprove\": [\n        \"read-neo4j-cypher\",\n        \"write-neo4j-cypher\",\n        \"get-neo4j-schema\"\n      ]\n    },\n    \"code-analyzer-mcp\": {\n      \"command\": \"node\",\n      \"args\": [\n        \"c:/code/amcp/mcp/dist/index.js\"\n      ],\n      \"cwd\": \"c:/code/amcp/mcp\",\n      \"disabled\": false,\n      \"alwaysAllow\": [\n        \"run_analyzer\",\n        \"start_watcher\",\n        \"stop_watcher\"\n      ]\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\n## 🛠️ Installation and Prerequisites\n\n### Prerequisites\n- **Neo4j Database**: Tested with Neo4j Desktop v5.26.4 (CLI)\n\n```bash\n# Navigate to the project directory\ncd c:/code/amcp\n\n# Run the analyzer (using compiled code in dist/)\n# Replace <path/to/your/codebase> with the actual path\nnode dist/index.js [L2]   "content": "# Security Policy\n\nSynapse gives an AI agent a real local computer-use body: it can move the mouse,\ntype, press keys, run allowlisted shell commands, launch processes, capture the\nscreen, and read accessibility trees. Treat it as a\npowerful, security-sensitive tool and run it only on machines and accounts where\nthat level of control is acceptable.\n\n## Reporting a vulnerability\n\n**Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues,\ndiscussions, or pull requests.**\n\nInstead, report privately:\n\n- Preferred: open a [GitHub private security advisory](https://github.com/ChrisRoyse/Synapse/security/advisories/new)\n  (\"Report a vulnerability\").\n- Or email **chrisroyseai@gmail.com** with subject `SECURITY: Synapse`.\n\nPlease include:\n\n- A description of the issue and its impact.\n- Steps to reproduce, or a proof of concept.\n- Affected version / commit, OS, and configuration.\n- Any suggested remediation.\n\nYou can expect an acknowledgement within a few days. Please give a reasonable\nopportunity to investigate and ship a fix before any public disclosure. Reports\nmade in good faith are welcome and appreciated.\n\n## Scope and operational guidance\n\nBecause Synapse is designed to control the local machine, the following are\n**expected behavior**, not vulnerabilities, when configured by the operator:\n\n- Sending input (keyboard/mouse) to the focused application.\n- Capturing the screen and reading UI Automation / accessibility data.\n- Running shell commands and launching processes that the operator has\n  explicitly allowlisted.\n\nGenuine security issues include, for example: bypassing the configured\nallowlists or safety gates, privilege escalation, authentication bypass on the\nHTTP transport, leaking secrets/credentials into logs or stored rows, or remote\ncode execution beyond the operator's configured surface.\n\n### Hardening recommendations\n\n- Run the HTTP transport bound to loopback (`127.0.0.1`) only, and set\n  `SYNAPSE_BEARER_TOKEN` to a strong value.\n- Run under a least-privilege user account dedicated to automation.\n- Keep allowlists for `act_run_shell` / `act_launch` as narrow as possible.\n- Do not expose the server to untrusted networks.\n",

D1 still requires manual MCP calls and separate Source-of-Truth reads before accepting any shipped behavior.\n\nThe matrix covers the general computer-use action, perception, session, target, lease, reflex, and diagnostic MCP tools. Domain-specific profile, storage, audit-export, and replay tools are outside this matrix unless they directly own foreground, cursor, target, or background computer-control state.\n\nStatus values:\n\n- `background-pass`: current implementation has a background or per-session path that does not need global foreground or cursor.\n- `conditional-pass`: current implementation has a background path for some target forms and a declared leased foreground path for the rest.\n- `foreground-capable-targeted`: current implementation can operate on a session-owned target even when that target is active/highlighted/focused, without falling back to an unrelated human foreground target.\n- `foreground-lease`: current implementation intentionally uses the shared foreground resource and must be lease-gated.\n- `gap-linked`: current implementation has a known multi-agent/background gap, and the follow-up issue is named here.\n- `control`: session, lease, reflex, or target control surface with no direct foreground action.\n- `diagnostic`: test-only operational diagnostic surface, not a user workflow primitive.\n- `sessionless`: no window or cursor state is used, but the resource is not session-owned.\n\nModel-selection exposure values:\n\n- `normal_agent`: the literal tool name/schema is visible in the default HTTP MCP profile.\n- `facade_only`: the raw implementation tool name/schema is hidden from the default profile, but the capability is reachable through a named public facade in the 40-tool surface.\n- `browser_debugger`: the stable `browser_debugger` facade is visible in the default profile so static MCP clients keep one callable route; its raw-CDP and `chrome.debugger` operations fail closed until an explicit `tool_profile_set browser_debugger` transition with confirm + reason.\n- `break_glass`: legacy classification for a raw OS/global implementation primitive. System Overview\n\n**Source files covered:**\n- `Cargo.toml` (workspace root), `clippy.toml`, `deny.toml`\n- `README.md`\n- `crates/synapse-mcp/src/main.rs`, `server.rs`, `m1.rs`, `m2.rs`, `m3.rs`, `m4.rs`, `single_instance.rs`, `daemon_lifecycle.rs`\n- `crates/synapse-core/src/lib.rs`, `defaults.rs`, `error_codes.rs`\n- The 14 workspace crates' `lib.rs` / `main.rs` module declarations\n- Synthesized from companion documents 02–17 in this series\n\n> Scope note: every claim below is derived from source in the `C:\\code\\synapse` workspace. Where a fact is documented in detail elsewhere in this series it is cross-referenced rather than repeated.\n\n---\n\n## 1. What the system is\n\nSynapse is a local **Model Context Protocol (MCP) server**, written in Rust (edition 2024, `rust-version = 1.95`), that gives an LLM agent a structured interface to a **Windows** PC: it perceives the screen (capture + OCR + object detection + accessibility tree), emits human-like mouse/keyboard/gamepad input, runs sub-millisecond reflex loops, drives the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, and orchestrates a fleet of agents that share one machine. It speaks MCP over stdio and over HTTP/SSE, and is designed to plug into Claude Code, Codex, and the Claude Desktop app (`README.md`).\n\nThe system is structured as a Cargo workspace of **14 crates** (`Cargo.toml`). `synapse-mcp` is the server/daemon and the sink of the dependency graph; `synapse-core` is the shared-vocabulary root with no internal dependencies. See [02_source_code_map.md](02_source_code_map.md) for the full crate tree and dependency graph.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Runtime / process & port topology\n\nThe product runs as a single canonical daemon plus subordinate processes spawned by CLI `--mode`. The daemon enforces single-instance ownership via an `fs2` advisory lock on `<db>/daemon.lock` (PID sidecar `daemon.pid`); a duplicate launch exits with code 3 and is told to use `--mode connect` (`crates/synapse-mcp/src/single_instance.rs`, `main.rs`).\n\n| Process / role | How launched | Transport / port | Technology | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| MCP daemon (stdio) | `--mode stdio` (default) | stdio JSON-RPC | `rmcp` 1.7.0 | Primary MCP server for a directly-attached client |\n| MCP daemon (HTTP) | `--mode http` | `127.0.0.1:7700` (`DEFAULT_BIND`) | axum 0.8 + `rmcp` StreamableHttpService at `/mcp`; SSE at `/events` | Shared daemon for multiple agents; bearer-token auth |\n| Connect shim | `--mode connect` | → 7700 | — | Bridges a stdio client into the already-running shared daemon |\n| Desktop worker | `--mode desktop-worker` | IPC to daemon | Win32 | Runs in an interactive desktop session for input/capture |\n| Local agent | `--mode local-agent` | IPC | — | Hosts a locally-spawned sub-agent |\n| Chrome native host | `--mode chrome-native-host` (bin `synapse-chrome-native-host`) | Chrome native messaging (stdio) | MV3 extension bridge | Backs the CDP bridge for the installed Chrome extension |\n| Approval protocol helper | `--mode approval-protocol` | URI handler | — | Handles `synapse://` approval callbacks |\n| Doctor | `--mode doctor` | — | — | Diagnostics; kills stray `synapse-mcp` processes |\n| Overlay | separate binary `synapse-overlay` | polls daemon HTTP every 2 s | Win32 `Shell_NotifyIconW` tray | System-tray status companion (recorder/demo/approvals/sessions/lease) |\n\nDefault `--mode` is `Stdio` (env `SYNAPSE_MODE`). Gate: `admission`, `superiority`, `risk`, `oracle`, `wash`, `policy`, and `policy_audit` refuse\n   unsafe, stale, ungrounded, uncalibrated, or trading-related actions.\n7. [L2]   "content": "# Building on Calyx — The Complete Builder's & Agent's Handbook\n\n**What this is.** A self‑contained, domain‑neutral, deep reference for building *any* intelligent system on top of **Calyx**, applicable to *any* project and *any* domain — fraud/risk, clinical registries, IoT/sensor fleets, product catalogs, log/observability pipelines, recommendation, scientific corpora, document management, and anything else with a corpus and outcomes. Hand it to a person or to an AI agent and they will understand what Calyx is, everything it can do, the exact math it bakes in, the single most important design decision (embeddings vs. structured encoding), how to combine both, and the disciplined method for extracting maximum grounded intelligence. Constants and formulas below are Calyx's own; treat them as defaults you can tune.\n\n> **Calyx in one sentence.** Calyx is an **association‑native database**: its native record is a **constellation** — one input measured through a *panel* of many independent frozen **lenses**, each producing its own typed vector kept separate (never flattened) — and on top of that record it bakes in the whole \"formula for intelligence\": it counts the **associations between** lenses, measures in **bits** which lenses carry real signal about outcomes, distills the minimal **kernel** that explains a corpus, **guards** generation against out‑of‑distribution drift, **predicts** consequences, and **self‑optimizes** — all in‑process, deterministic, no external services.\n\n> ## ★ THE FOUNDATIONAL PRINCIPLE — read this before anything else\n>\n> **Building on Calyx means committing to first principles.** You must decompose the *entire* project into its **atomic, irreducible, independently‑measurable units**, and then compute **ALL** associations among them **from the ground up** — every base relationship, not a sampled, assumed, or hand‑picked subset. This is the *only* way to **truly understand** a system, and this exhaustive ground‑up association structure **is the information Calyx actually derives its intelligence from.**\n>\n> Records are inert. A row, a document, a value — on its own it carries almost no intelligence. **The complete web of associations among the atoms is the raw material of intelligence.** Everything else in this handbook — bits, sufficiency, the kernel, the guard, the oracle, self‑optimization — is a way of *measuring, distilling, and composing* that ground‑up association structure. The kernel is its compressed generator; the bits are its grounded weights; the guard, oracle, and answers are built *from* it.\n>\n> **Therefore, never shortcut it.** If you skip the decomposition to atoms, or leave base associations uncomputed, the intelligence you extract is partial, biased, and ungrounded — you will have measured a shadow of the system, not the system. The discipline is always the same: **atoms → all base associations → differentiate → kernel → compose.** Decompose everything; compute every association from the ground up; only then does Calyx have the full information it needs to derive maximum grounded intelligence.\n>\n> **The no-collapse law is absolute. A kernel member is a constellation, never a vector.** Every graph, kernel index, guard, Answer, ledger record, reproduce path, and estimator transport MUST preserve the complete contracted slot map with each lens output typed, separate, and addressable. The declared shape is part of that contract: `Multi` remains token-level `Multi` and uses native late-interaction/MaxSim semantics; mean/max pooling it into one dense vector is not preservation. Joint estimators consume an ordered set of explicit lens blocks and may traverse those blocks in one calculation, but MUST NOT concatenate them into a substitute record. Conditioning is fitted per lens block on training data only, and its block roster, dimensions, fold identities, and scales are persisted as provenance. Missing or mismatched block boundaries fail closed. A scalar association or rank-fusion score is permitted only as a derived value whose per-slot evidence remains present; it never replaces the constellation. Selecting one preferred lens, serializing one vector per kernel member, pooling a typed multi-vector slot, flattening/concatenating the panel, or recording only the fused score is a foundational system failure and MUST fail closed.\n\n**How to read this.** §1–§4 are the model. §5 is the core decision (embed vs. encode) and the single most important section for structured data. §6 is the extraction *method*. §7 is the subsystem‑by‑subsystem deep reference with the math. §8–§9 are interfaces and recipes. §10 shows the same mechanics across many domains. §11 is tuning/ops. §12–§14 are doctrine, a formulas/constants/errors reference, and a glossary.\n\n---\n\n## 1. What Calyx is\n\n**The thesis.** Calyx is \"the formula for intelligence, implemented as a database.\" Three things in one: (1) the engine of a **calculus of association** — four native verbs; (2) a **universal database** that serves every paradigm's root purpose on one ordered transactional core; (3) an **oracle/kernel substrate** for grounded prediction and knowledge.\n\n**The native record is not a row or a vector — it is a constellation.** One input, measured through a *panel* of many frozen instruments (\"lenses\"), each producing its own typed slot‑vector that is **kept separate and never concatenated into one opaque blob**. On top of that record Calyx bakes in association‑counting, information‑theoretic measurement, kernel discovery, a fail‑closed guard, a provenance ledger, reversible self‑optimization, and grounded consequence prediction.\n\n**The four verbs** (this is the whole pipeline):\n\n| Verb | Meaning | What it produces |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Measure** | view one input through a panel of lenses | a constellation (many typed slots) |\n| **Count** | derive the associations *between* slots and between records | cross‑terms, an agreement graph, a between‑record graph |\n| **Differentiate** | quantify the unique **bits** each lens/association adds about a real outcome | signal in bits, sufficiency, redundancy, causality |\n| **Compose** | find the kernel, guard generation, answer, predict, self‑optimize | index, answers, guard verdicts, predictions, tuned params |\n\n**Three trust principles, enforced in code:**\n- **Grounding is mandatory.** Claims are measured against *anchored real outcomes*. Anything not grounded is tagged **provisional**, never \"trusted.\"\n- **No‑flatten / no‑collapse.** Slots stay typed and separate end‑to‑end, including their declared `Dense` / `Sparse` / `Multi` shape through graph, index, truth, kernel, Answer, ledger, and reproduction. A `Multi` slot is never pooled into one dense vector; a path without native MaxSim support fails closed. The guard scores each slot independently. Derived association/fusion scores retain every slot's contribution and never become a substitute record.\n- **Fail closed.** Unknown lens, shape mismatch, uncalibrated guard, missing data, non‑finite value ⇒ a **structured error** (`{code, message, remediation}`), never a silent wrong answer.\n\n**The living‑system map** (each life‑like property maps to a concrete engine): perception = lenses · memory = the store · cognition = associations + search · differentiation = the bits engine · homeostasis = the self‑optimizer · foresight = the oracle · immune boundary = the guard. Calyx claims *operational* intelligence and life‑like behavior — never consciousness.\n\n---\n\n## 2. When to use Calyx, and the universality claim\n\n**Universality principle.** Serve the root purpose of **every** data paradigm from first principles, not by bolting engines together:\n\n| You want… | In Calyx it is… | Mechanic |\n|---|---|---|\n| a **vector database** | a **1‑lens** Calyx | one embedder lens + ANN |\n| **full‑text search** | a **sparse lens** + BM25 | sparse slot + inverted index |\n| a **document / key‑value / columnar store** | collections over one ordered core | scalars + metadata + column families |\n| a **graph database** | the association graph + traversal | cross‑terms + between‑record edges + best‑first walk |\n| a **time‑series store** | recurrence series + temporal lenses | event series + recency/periodic/positional |\n| a **feature store / analytics** | slots + scalars + measured bits | encoders + mutual information |\n| **retrieval + reranking** | multi‑lens fusion + a reranker lens | RRF + cross‑encoder |\n| an **agent's memory / knowledge layer** | constellations + kernel + oracle + ledger | the whole stack |\n\n**Reach for Calyx** when you need *grounded intelligence over a corpus*: semantic recall, \"which features actually matter (in bits)\", relationship discovery, deduplication, anomaly detection, grounded question‑answering, consequence prediction, imputation, forecasting, or provenance — and you want it embedded, deterministic, and free.\n\n**Do not reach for Calyx** when a plain transactional row‑store with no intelligence requirement is all you need and you will never ask an association/bits/kernel/guard/oracle question — although even then, Calyx's universal core can serve the row‑store role.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Core concepts in depth\n\n**Lens.** A frozen, content‑addressed measurement instrument implementing `measure(input) -> vector`. Examples span every modality: a text embedder, an image encoder, a numeric normalizer, a one‑hot encoder, a temporal decay, a graph‑structural signature. **Invariants:** a lens is *frozen* — its weights/spec never change; if the runtime drifts, that becomes a **new** lens id, never a silent reuse. Its identity is a hash of `(name, weights, corpus, output‑shape)`. Adding a lens is *one call*; its worth is *one number* (bits). This \"plug‑in lens is the key\" property is sacred — never make it harder.\n\n**Slot.** One lens's typed output vector inside a record, addressed by a stable slot id and a human‑readable key. Slots carry lifecycle state (active / parked / retired), a quantization policy, an optional axis tag, and flags like *retrieval‑only* (used post‑retrieval, not for primary recall) and *excluded‑from‑dedup*. **Slots stay separate — never flattened.**\n\n**Panel.** A versioned set of slots — the lenses you measure every input through. Panels are **hot‑swappable**: `add_lens` bumps the version and enqueues **lazy backfill** (old records fill in the background; new records are searchable immediately). Park/retire transitions are non‑destructive; retired slots stay readable for history.\n\n**Constellation.** One input measured through the panel = the atomic record. It carries the typed slots, exact scalar measurements, verbatim metadata, grounded anchors, and a provenance reference. Its id is a content address of `(input bytes, panel version, vault salt)` — so identical input under the same panel yields the same id ⇒ **idempotency**.\n\n**Anchor.** A grounded real‑outcome observation attached to a record: a label, a reward, a pass/tie/thumbs, an identity/style hold, or a recurrence, with a source and a confidence. **Bits are measured *about* anchors.** An anchor is \"grounded\" iff its source is non‑blank and its confidence is finite in `(0,1]`. Without grounded anchors, every bits/sufficiency result is **provisional**.\n\n**Cross‑term.** A derived association between two slots (agreement / delta / interaction / concat). Between records, associations become **edges** in a nearest‑neighbor graph. The cross‑term is the atom of \"counting.\"\n\n**Kernel.** The minimal generating core of a corpus — the small set of **complete constellations** (a feedback‑vertex‑set, on the order of ~1%) from which the rest of the corpus's intelligence can be reconstructed. Every kernel member retains the full contracted panel as a typed slot map; a one-vector kernel is invalid. The kernel doubles as an index and an answer path, and can be computed at **any scope**.\n\n**Guard.** The per‑slot, fail‑closed, conformally‑calibrated gate that decides whether a query/output is inside the trusted region — per slot, never averaged.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Data model\n\n- **Constellation** — `{ id, vault_id, panel_version, created_at, input_ref, modality, slots: map<slot_id, slot_vector>, scalars: map<string,f64>, metadata: map<string,string>, anchors: [anchor], provenance, flags }`. Validated fail‑closed: panel version > 0, every slot vector valid, scalar values finite, non‑empty keys, every anchor valid.\n- **Slot vector shapes** — `Dense{dim, data}` · `Sparse{dim, entries:[{idx,val}]}` · `Multi{token_dim, tokens:[[..]]}` (multi‑vector / late interaction) · `Absent{reason}`. **`Absent` is an explicit absence — never interpret it as a zero vector.** Validation: dense length == dim and finite; sparse indices in range, no duplicates; multi tokens all == token_dim.\n- **Modality** — the accepted input kinds: `Text, Code, Image, Audio, Video, Structured, Mixed`, plus scientific modalities (protein/DNA/molecule). **`Structured` is first‑class**, and records natively carry `scalars` (exact numeric measurements) and `metadata` (verbatim strings) so you keep exact values alongside vectors.\n- **Anchor** — `{ kind, value, source, observed_at, confidence∈[0,1] }`. Kinds cover labels, rewards, pass/tie/thumbs, identity/style holds, and recurrence. Values: bool / number / enum / one‑hot / text / vector.\n- **Signal** — a measured bits result: `{ bits, confidence_interval, n_samples, estimator, timestamp }`. Each slot carries a `bits_about` map (per outcome axis).\n- **Identity & determinism.** All ids are content addresses: a 128‑bit hash over **length‑delimited ordered parts** (so `[\"ab\",\"c\"]` ≠ `[\"a\",\"bc\"]`). Lens id = hash of `(name, weights_sha, corpus_hash, output_shape)`; record id = hash of `(input_bytes, panel_version_be, vault_salt)`. Determinism and idempotency fall out for free; a determinism probe requires byte‑identical repeat output.\n- **Extension traits.** Implement `Lens` (measure), `Index` (ANN/inverted), `VaultStore` (storage), or `Estimator` (information measures) to extend the engine. All are object‑safe and `Send + Sync`.\n\n---\n\n## 5. THE CORE DECISION — embeddings vs. structured encoding (the most important section)\n\nFor any input you ask: **do I derive meaning by embedding raw bytes into a vector, or by treating the explicit fields directly?** This one choice determines whether your intelligence is grounded and cheap or fuzzy and noisy.\n\n### 5.1 The principle — where does the meaning live?\n\n- **Unstructured — text, images, audio, video, code, scientific sequences.** The meaning is *latent in the raw bytes*; a pixel or a byte is not itself the concept. You **must** use a learned **embedder lens** to project into a vector where **geometry = meaning** (cosine ≈ semantic distance). \"Association\" here = nearness in embedding space; you retrieve with approximate nearest neighbors and fuse with rank fusion.\n- **Structured — tables, records, fields: numbers, categories, booleans, ordinals, timestamps, references.** The meaning is *already explicit*. A duration of `42`, a status of `active`, a flag `true` already **are** the concept. You should **not** run a learned embedder over them, because it (a) destroys the exact, auditable value, (b) replaces information theory (the right tool) with cosine geometry (the wrong one), and (c) forfeits Calyx's ability to measure the association between a field and an outcome **directly, in bits**. \"Association\" here = **statistical dependence** (mutual information, correlation, transfer entropy), not geometric nearness.\n\n> **Rule of thumb:** *Embed what is latent; encode what is explicit; measure both against grounded anchors in bits so they live on one axis.* Never embed a value that is already meaningful.\n\n### 5.2 Every way to *use* structured data (deterministic encoders — no learned embedder)\n\nEach becomes a frozen lens → a slot. Apply as many as fit; more diverse encodings ⇒ more captured associations.\n\n**Per‑field value encoders**\n1. **Scalar normalization variants** (each its own lens on the same field):\n   - `raw` (as‑is, for already‑bounded values);\n   - `min‑max` → `(x−min)/(max−min)` into `[0,1]`;\n   - `z‑score` → `(x−μ)/σ`;\n   - `log / log1p` → `sign(x)·log(1+|x|)` for heavy tails / multiplicative scales;\n   - `rank / quantile` → the

Built with **Three.js** and **TypeScript**, this project brings AI agents to life in a mesmerizing 3D environment, where they interact and evolve in real-time. Each agent follows a leader, forming a chain of movement with oscillating trails, all rendered directly in your browser using WebGL.\n\n---\n\n## Features\n\n- **Real-time 3D Visualization**: Watch AI agents move and interact in a flowing, dynamic pattern.\n- **Agent Behavior**: Agents follow a leader in a chain, creating a snake-like movement with oscillating trails.\n- **Unique Visuals**: Each agent has a distinct color and leaves a fading trail, adding depth and beauty to the scene.\n- **Screen Wrapping**: Agents seamlessly reappear on the opposite side when they move off-screen, creating a continuous environment.\n- **Tech Stack**:\n  - **Three.js**: For WebGL rendering, enabling smooth and performant 3D graphics in the browser.\n  - **TypeScript**: For type safety and better development experience.\n  - **Vite**: For fast development and building, providing instant feedback during development.\n\n---\n\n## Installation\n\nTo get started with the Living AI Agent System, follow these steps:\n\n### Prerequisites\n\nEnsure you have the following installed:\n- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) (version 14 or higher recommended)\n- [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) (comes with Node.js)\n\n### Steps\n\n1. **Clone the Repository**:\n   ```bash\n   git clone https://github.com/yourusername/livingai.git\n   ```\n   *Replace `yourusername` with your actual GitHub username.*\n\n2. **Navigate to the Project Directory**:\n   ```bash\n   cd livingai\n   ```\n\n3. **Install Dependencies**:\n   ```bash\n   npm install\n   ```\n   This will install all required packages, including Three.js, TypeScript, and Vite, as specified in `package.json`.\n\n---\n\n## Usage\n\nOnce installed, you can run the project in various modes:\n\n### Development Mode\n\nStart the development server to view the visualization in real-time:\n```bash\nnpm run dev\n```\n- This launches a server at `http://localhost:6873`.\n- The page updates automatically as you make changes to the code, thanks to Vite's hot module replacement.\n\n### Build for Production\n\nCreate an optimized production build:\n```bash\nnpm run build\n```\n- This compiles the TypeScript code and bundles the assets into the `dist` folder.\n- The build is optimized for performance and ready for deployment.\n\n### Preview the Build\n\nServe the production build locally to test it:\n```bash\nnpm run preview\n```\n- This starts a local server to preview the contents of the `dist` folder.\n\n---\n\n## How It Works\n\nThe Living AI Agent System simulates a chain of AI agents, each following the one before it, creating a flowing, organic movement. The agents are rendered as colored spheres with trails that fade over time, adding a sense of motion and depth to the visualization.\n\n### Scene Setup\n\n- The scene is initialized using Three.js, with a black background (`0x000000`) for contrast.\n- A perspective camera is used, positioned at `z = 30` to provide a clear view of the agents.\n- The WebGL renderer is set up with antialiasing for smooth edges and full-screen rendering.\n\n### EcoAgent Class\n\nEach agent is an instance of the `EcoAgent` class, defined in `main.ts`. The class manages the following properties and behaviors:\n\n#### Properties\n\n- **Position** (`THREE.Vector3`): The current location of the agent in 3D space.\n- **Velocity** (`THREE.Vector3`): The direction and speed of movement.\n- **Trail** (`THREE.Vector3[]`): An array of past positions, used to render the agent's trail.\n- **Color** (`THREE.Color`): A unique color for the agent and its trail.\n- **Leader** (`EcoAgent | null`): The agent this instance follows, if any.\n- **Followers** (`EcoAgent[]`): List of agents following this instance.\n- **Phase** (`number`): Used for oscillation in movement, adding natural variation.\n\n#### Constructor\n\n- Initializes the agent with a random starting position and velocity.\n- Assigns a unique color and sets up the trail with the starting position.\n- Randomizes the phase for oscillation effects.\n\n#### Update Method\n\nThe `update` method is called each frame to update the agent's position and behavior:\n\n- **If the Agent Has a Leader (Follower Behavior)**:\n  - Targets a point in the leader's trail (10 steps behind, or the leader's current position if the trail is shorter).\n  - Calculates the direction to the target and normalizes it.\n  - Adds oscillation by computing a perpendicular vector and scaling it with a sine function, creating a wavy, natural motion.\n  - Adjusts speed based on distance to the leader, ensuring smooth following behavior.\n  - Updates velocity using linear interpolation (`lerp`) for gradual changes.\n\n- **If the Agent Is a Leader (No Leader)**:\n  - Moves in a flowing pattern using sine and cosine functions for the x and y directions.\n  - Updates velocity using `lerp` for smooth transitions.\n\n- **Position Update**:\n  - Adds the velocity to the position to move the agent.\n  - Implements screen wrapping:\n    - If the agent moves beyond ±30 units in x or y, it reappears on the opposite side.\n    - This creates a continuous, boundary-less environment.\n\n- **Trail Update**:\n  - Adds the current position to the trail.\n  - Limits the trail to 50 points, removing the oldest point if necessary.\n\n### Agent Chain Setup\n\n- 25 agents are created with random starting positions and colors.\n- The agents are connected in a chain:\n  - The first agent (index 0) is the leader and has no leader.\n  - Each subsequent agent follows the previous one (e.g., agent 1 follows agent 0, agent 2 follows agent 1, etc.).\n  - Leaders store references to their followers, forming a bidirectional chain.\n\n### Rendering\n\n- **Agent Meshes**:\n  - Each agent is represented as a sphere (`THREE.SphereGeometry`, radius 0.2, 16 segments).\n  - Uses `THREE.MeshBasicMaterial` with the agent's unique color.\n  - Added to the scene and updated each frame with the agent's position.\n\n- **Trail Lines**:\n  - Each trail is rendered as a line (`THREE.Line`) using `THREE.BufferGeometry`.\n  - The trail geometry is updated each frame with the agent's trail positions.\n  - Uses `THREE.LineBasicMaterial` with:\n    - The agent's color.\n    - Transparency (`opacity: 0.5`) and additive blending for a glowing, fading effect.\n\n- **Animation Loop**:\n  - Runs continuously using `requestAnimationFrame`.\n  - Updates each agent's position and trail using the `EcoAgent` class.\n  - Updates the corresponding mesh and trail line in the scene.\n  - Renders the scene with the camera using the WebGL renderer.\n\n---\n\n## Configuration\n\nYou can customize the simulation by modifying the following in `main.ts`:\n\n### Number of Agents\n\n- Adjust the loop that creates the agents:\n  ```typescript\n  for (let i = 0; i < 25; i++) {\n  ```\n  - Change `25` to the desired number of agents.\n  - Note: Each agent after the first will follow the previous one, forming a longer or shorter chain.\n\n### Screen Bounds\n\n- Modify the `bounds` variable:\n  ```typescript\n  const bounds = 30;\n  ```\n  - This sets the wrapping area to ±30 units in x and y.\n  - Increase or decrease this value to change the size of the visible area.\n\n### Other Potential Adjustments\n\n- **Agent Size**: Modify the sphere geometry in the rendering section (e.g., change the radius from 0.2).\n- **Trail Length**: Adjust the trail limit in the `update` method (e.g., change `50` to a different number).\n- **Movement Speed**: Adjust the speed factors in the `update` method (e.g., `speed = THREE.MathUtils.clamp(distance * 0.1, 0.05, 0.2)`).\n- **Oscillation Amplitude/Frequency**: Modify the oscillation parameters in the follower behavior (e.g., change `Math.sin(time * 0.002 + this.phase) * 0.5`).\n\n---\n\n## Project Structure\n\nThe project is organized as follows:\n\n- **`src/main.ts`**: Core logic, including the `EcoAgent` class, scene setup, and animation loop.\n- **`src/style.css`**: Minimal CSS for full-screen rendering:\n  - Resets margins and padding.\n  - Hides overflow to ensure the visualization fills the screen.\n- **`index.html`**: Basic HTML structure linking the CSS and TypeScript files.\n- **`vite-env.d.ts`**: Type definitions for Vite environment variables (currently unused).\n- **`vite.config.ts`**: Vite configuration, specifying the development server port (6873) and build target (`esnext`).\n- **`tsconfig.json`**: TypeScript configuration, enabling strict type checking and ESNext modules.\n- **`package.json`**: Project metadata, scripts, and dependencies.\n\n---\n\n## Dependencies\n\nThe project uses the following dependencies (listed in `package.json`):\n\n### Runtime Dependencies\n\n- **`three`**: For 3D rendering with WebGL.\n- **`typescript`**: For type-safe development.\n- **`@types/node`**: Type definitions for Node.js (used by TypeScript).\n- **`dspy.ts`**: Not currently used in the provided code; possibly for future AI integration.\n- **`onnxruntime-web`**: Not currently used; possibly for future machine learning model execution.\n\n### Development Dependencies\n\n- **`@types/three`**: Type definitions for Three.js.\n- **`vite`**: Fast build tool and development server.\n\nNote: Dependencies like `dspy.ts` and `onnxruntime-web` are not used in the current implementation.
