===== GMRI_Public_Research_2026-10-28/knowledge_system/reports/CORRECTED_COUNTS_AND_METHOD.md =====
# Reconciled evidence counts and measurement method

Date: 2026-10-28. These are **read-only aggregate queries** against GMRI's private SQLite evidence database; none of its rows are in this public packet. The source ZIP for the 2026 snapshot was unavailable for independent source-level rebuilding; the SQLite database passed integrity checks, which do not prove source-level completeness.

| Unit | Snapshot records / appearances | Distinct identities | Meaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Messages | 31,041 | 28,644 | Stable `(conversation_id,message_id)` identity; ancillary thread treated separately |
| Attachment metadata references | 2,288 | 2,184 | Snapshot-level reference versus message/attachment identity |
| Asset-pointer records, **including synthetic** | 2,339 | 2,312 | Includes generated `attachment://` pointers; not solely embedded pointers |
| Citation records | 21,185 | 19,116 | Same message, URL, and title not independent per snapshot |

**Asset resolution denominator correction:** 1,505 pointers embedded in source messages; 891 matched at least one packaged-file candidate (**59.2%**). Another 834 rows are generated from attachment matches. Combining them yields the earlier 1,725/2,339 count but must never be presented as the embedded-pointer resolution rate. A file match is not independently verified semantic identity.

**Text extraction coverage:** 6,087 of 28,644 canonical message records currently have zero extracted searchable characters. This does **not** establish that meaningful text was missed in all such records: empty placeholders and non-text content may be legitimate. Until a stratified raw-payload comparison is completed, extraction recall is **unmeasured**. Do not use search hit counts as hazard incidence.

**Conversation identity coverage:** 350 distinct provider conversations plus 1 ancillary thread; 2023/2024 snapshots overlap, while the 2026 snapshot shares no conversation IDs with 2024. The latter is a **record discontinuity**; deletion, account/workspace change, export retention/scope, and genuinely absent activity are competing explanations. The latest exported conversation is from **2026-03-25**; the data do not cover later 2026 research conversations.

**Historical checks:** the earlier report's `18 passes, 2 warnings` is a recorded self-consistency result from the original validator. Its checks operate primarily on builder-created tables and indices and must not be described as independent source-level corroboration. No hazard prevalence, causal mechanism, rate of external events, or extinction probability is estimated from these counts.

**SQL identity expressions used:**

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM messages;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM message_appearances;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM attachments;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
  SELECT conversation_id,message_id,
         COALESCE(NULLIF(attachment_id,''), name,''), COALESCE(mime_type,'')
  FROM attachments GROUP BY 1,2,3,4
);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM asset_pointers;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
  SELECT conversation_id,message_id,pointer
  FROM asset_pointers GROUP BY 1,2,3
);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM asset_pointers
 WHERE pointer NOT LIKE 'attachment://%' AND resolution_status='resolved';
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM asset_pointers WHERE pointer NOT LIKE 'attachment://%';
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM citations;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
  SELECT conversation_id,message_id,url,COALESCE(title,'')
  FROM citations GROUP BY 1,2,3,4
);
```

**Provenance classifications:** SQL aggregates computed locally from the existing private database = **calculated**; original source-level recount of all snapshots = **not performed**; source contents and all purported external events = **require separately identified evidence**. The supplied threat model itself is not reduced to these archive counts.

===== GMRI_Public_Research_2026-10-28/knowledge_system/reports/INDEPENDENT_SOURCE_RECOUNT_PARTIAL.md =====
# Independent raw-source recount: 2023 and 2024 exports

**Executed locally 2026-10-28.** Two available original provider-export ZIPs were first hashed and confirmed byte-for-byte identical to the hashes in the private source registry. Their bytes are not published. The recount uses a new source-only script, `scripts/independent_source_recount.py`, which does **not** call the corpus builder or read SQLite.

| Raw export | Conversations | Message-bearing mapping nodes | Distinct `(conversation_id, message_id)` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| November 2023 | 57 | 2,406 | 2,406 |
| August 2024 | 238 | 11,142 | **11,142** |
| Combined, after overlapping-ID reconciliation | **241** | 13,548 raw appearances | **11,151** |

The two exports share 54 conversation IDs and 2,397 stable message identities. These results independently reproduce the earlier published appearance totals and conversation overlap. They also exposed a **one-record error in the original 2024 `distinct_message_ids` snapshot field**: it reported 11,141 instead of 11,142, because the original snapshot counter grouped by message ID alone rather than the compound `(conversation_id,message_id)` identity. The release code now uses the compound identity. This correction does not change the main private database's canonical total; the private DB remains untouched.

**Independent source-level coverage is incomplete.** The March 2026 original provider-export ZIP is not available in this working environment. The 2026 snapshot, and hence the combined three-snapshot count of 28,568 provider messages (28,644 including the ancillary group thread), has **not** been independently recounted from its original source export. The complete database may be checked structurally and via SQL, but that is a different claim.

This recount concerns identities, not the semantic correctness or clinical, institutional, or physical-world claims made inside the messages.

===== GMRI_Public_Research_2026-10-28/knowledge_system/docs/07_LONGITUDINAL_METHOD.md =====
# Longitudinal Method

## Research posture

This corpus is suitable for a longitudinal case archive, retrospective process tracing, and exploratory threat-model research. It is not a representative sample of OpenAI users, and the exports do not prove that provider history is exhaustive.

The study should be designed to answer questions that the archive can actually observe.

## 1. Define the unit of analysis

Choose one primary unit before coding:

- conversation;
- message identity;
- user-assistant turn exchange;
- active-path episode;
- reported incident;
- model/tool action;
- external event;
- threat case.

A message-level count answers a different question from a conversation-level or incident-level count. Do not mix them.

Recommended starting units:

| Question type | Primary unit |
|---|---|
| Longitudinal language or topic change | distinct conversation and sampled message identities |
| Question fidelity | exact question/restatement pair |
| Verification failure | verification claim with receipt status |
| Access interruption | reported or externally confirmed interruption episode |
| Threat pathway | evidence-linked multi-step case |
| Prevalence | not supported by this archive alone |

## 2. Freeze the analysis frame

Document:

- source snapshots;
- hash values;
- date range;
- included roles and content types;
- active-path or all-branch scope;
- treatment of tool and system messages;
- treatment of ancillary group threads;
- attachment inclusion rules;
- duplicate and overlap rules.

The current archive should state that the 2024 and 2026 exports do not overlap and that an 11-month activity gap is present.

## 3. Separate observation from coding

Use three layers.

### Source layer

Exact provider exports, hashes, message identities, raw message JSON.

### Coding layer

Researcher decisions such as:

- `question_restatement`;
- `verification_claim`;
- `correction`;
- `access_interruption`;
- `reported_harm`;
- `external_evidence_requested`;
- `institutional_recourse_reported`.

These are analytic constructs, not properties automatically encoded in the text.

### Interpretation layer

Mechanism, causal pathway, forecast, and normative implication.

Do not store the interpretation in the same field as the source observation.

## 4. Codebook discipline

Each code needs:

- label;
- definition;
- inclusion criteria;
- exclusion criteria;
- positive examples;
- near-miss examples;
- required source status;
- whether transcript language alone is sufficient;
- whether external verification is required;
- whether branch inspection is required.

Example:

```text
Code: QUESTION_SUBSTITUTION
Definition: A later model message represents a materially different investigative target as the original question.
Include: exact original question and later restatement, with the difference identified.
Exclude: a clarification that preserves the same target.
Do not infer: intent, deception, or prevalence.
```

## 5. LLM-assisted coding

An LLM may help retrieve and label candidates. It must not be the sole coder for a material claim.

Required safeguards:

1. Use a fixed codebook and output schema.
2. Retrieve context automatically.
3. Force stable references.
4. Require a counterevidence field.
5. Separate exact quotes from paraphrase.
6. Sample and human-code a validation subset.
7. Measure disagreement and correct the codebook.
8. Audit false positives and false negatives by source period.
9. Re-run after model or prompt changes.
10. Never report model self-agreement as human inter-rater reliability.

## 6. Snapshot reconciliation

For each conversation:

- compare provider metadata across snapshots;
- identify messages that appear, disappear, or change branch;
- keep all distinct message identities;
- report raw appearances and distinct identities;
- flag text conflicts rather than silently choosing one;
- treat HTML renders as derivatives.

The current build identifies 54 overlapping conversations, 2,397 overlapping message identities, 4,794 overlapping appearances, and zero extracted-text conflicts.

## 7. Temporal analysis

Use time as a causal dimension, not only a plotting axis.

Candidate time variables:

- conversation creation;
- message timestamp;
- snapshot observation date;
- model slug or release period;
- tool availability;
- reported institutional event date;
- correction date;
- recovery date.

Do not interpolate missing months. Report the gap.

# Independent-review findings and disposition (public release)

This document records a review of the **knowledge-system packaging and implementation**, not a peer review of the full scientific theory. Revisions are labeled explicitly; do not assume a test of source-processing code establishes a causal theory.

| Finding | Disposition for this release | Remaining work |
|---|---|---|
| Archive ordering by filesystem mtime | **Code patched + synthetic test**: ordering now uses dated source identifier with stable fallback | Rebuild private database when all original sources are authorized and available; compare identities |
| Raw vs distinct attachment/citation/asset counts | **Recomputed from private SQLite; publication corrected** | Original-source recount, independently implemented, to confirm all snapshots |
| Synthetic asset pointers inflated resolution metric | **Corrected**: embedded pointers resolved 891/1505; synthetic 834 separately | Validate semantic asset-file matches and coverage by match category |
| Validator uses builder-produced database | **Clarified; historical check no longer called independent** | Independent JSON-source parser / re-count, compare with DB |
| Inadequate overlap, asset, and conflict regression cases | **Partially corrected**: multi-snapshot source-order regression and schema tests; pre-existing synthetic build tests retained | Add multi-snapshot, group, asset, ZIP, and conflict fixtures before production rebuild |
| Missing root README, manifest mismatch | **Repaired in public release layout; regenerated manifest** | Re-check archive content after future changes |
| Text extraction recall unknown | **Reported explicitly**: zero-text rows counted; meaning not adjudicated | Stratified raw-payload extraction audit by content type, independent extractor |
| Snapshot distinct-ID counter grouped only by message ID | **Patched builder**: count `(conversation_id,message_id)`; independent 2024 recount confirmed a one-ID discrepancy in the original per-snapshot field | Original private DB remains unchanged; corrected count awaits rebuild |
| Two coverage-gap definitions | **Reconciled in published coverage note** | Establish single metric name for each gap definition in generator |
| Probe vocabulary differs across docs and JSON | **Declared alternate retrieval probes, not one-to-one executable definitions** | Version and freeze protocol queries in prospective evaluation |
| Evidence-status vocabularies not identical | **Public mapping note added** | Review backward compatibility and migration for private ledgers |
| Schemas permitted unjustified statuses | **Conditional JSON Schema constraints added + tests** | Human review remains necessary for substantive validity; migrate prior records if any |
| Public source metadata and local paths | **Removed from all shipped reports and documentation** | Human disclosure review and external reidentification threat-model check |
| Obsidian Sync enabled | **Sync disabled in shipped optional vault config** | Owner must verify Sync settings in any existing local/private vault |
| Group message synthetic flag and late report swap | **Group message ID flag patched**; late report swap still open | Test crash-safe report/database publishing transaction |
| Snapshot `--source` query and canonical conflict ambiguity | **Documented, not patched** | Return source-specific text in source-qualified query and add conflict fixtures |

These dispositions apply **only** to the distributed public code and documents. The private corpus has not been silently altered. No external cloud service was given the private records.

# GMRI GEV - OMP handoff

## Start

Extract this archive into a dedicated local directory on the machine running Oh My Pi. Keep the `.omp` directory intact. With OMP and its model access already configured, run from this directory:

```sh
omp @PRD.md "$(cat START.md)"
```

This supplies an explicit execution request and the full audited PRD. OMP reads project context from `.omp/AGENTS.md`; `.omp/RULES.md` carries short persistent reminders. Do not run the command from `.omp/` itself. Keep the executing workstation awake and the OMP session running while it works.

Use your already-authorized SSH access and existing runner permissions. This package does not log into Proxmox, grant tool access, change model/provider settings, or bypass approval controls. No passwords or tokens are included. A real access/permission blocker will be reported rather than bypassed.

## Files

- `.omp/AGENTS.md`: OMP execution instructions for the deployment.
- `.omp/RULES.md`: short persistent requirements for long sessions.
- `PRD.md`: complete body-text export of the already-audited deployment PRD, with code and table order preserved.
- `PRD_AUDIT_NOTES.md`: existing DOCX review comments, separate from the accepted specification.
- `START.md`: the initial execution request.
- `MANIFEST.sha256`: file-integrity hashes, not a signed provenance certificate or deployment result.

The original audited DOCX is unchanged and is not required for the bundled run. Its SHA-256 is recorded in the readable PRD and AGENTS.md. This package adds OMP workflow instructions; it does not re-audit or claim to have executed the hardware deployment.

For a standalone AGENTS.md download, save it as `.omp/AGENTS.md` in your deployment workspace and provide the exact audited PRD there. Preserve any existing instructions rather than overwriting them blindly. Do not put this host-specific mission in `~/.omp/agent/AGENTS.md`.

## Sources for OMP integration

Checked 2026-10-06 against the maintainer's published documentation. Use the installed `omp --help` for version-specific behavior.

- Context-file discovery and native persistent RULES.md: https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/blob/main/docs/context-files.md
- Initial prompts, `@file` attachments and execution modes: https://omp.sh/docs/cli
- Available tools and subagent capabilities: https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/blob/main/README.md

The AGENTS.md single-writer, bounded-delegation and checkpoint rules are authored operating instructions, not claims of automatic OMP enforcement. Authentication, model access, tool availability, workstation uptime and host capabilities still determine what the local run can execute.

The required baseline is keyless GEV plus the real GPU-driven internal-panel kiosk and trusted-network access. Keyless is not network-independent; provider outages must remain visible rather than replaced with simulated live data.

The collective can dynamically reallocate resources, navigate unforeseen obstacles, and optimize pathways to project goals.\n*   **🎯 Unambiguous AI-Verifiable Outcomes:** We move beyond subjective progress reports. Pheromind is architected to ensure that milestones are defined by outputs and states that can be programmatically verified by AI, bringing mathematical rigor to project tracking.\n*   **🗣️ Sophisticated Natural Language Interpretation:** Agents communicate and coordinate based on the interpretation of complex, narrative-style information, allowing for a richer and more flexible flow of understanding than rigid, predefined commands. This enables the swarm to react to nuanced updates and maintain a human-auditable trail of understanding.\n\n## 🔮 The Vision: The Pheromind AI IDE & Beyond\n\nPheromind is more than a framework; it's the blueprint for the **next generation of Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) – the AI IDE.**\n\nImagine an environment where:\n*   You define a high-level goal or user blueprint.\n*   A swarm of AI agents autonomously designs, codes, tests, and documents the software, adhering to best practices and your specific requirements.\n*   Progress is continuously verified, and the system adapts to challenges in real-time.\n*   Human developers transition to roles of high-level strategists, creative problem-solvers, and reviewers, amplified by an intelligent AI workforce.\n\nThe market for AI-assisted development tools is already valued in the **billions of dollars** with current solutions. [L2]   "content": "# calyx-poly\n\n`calyx-poly` is the local Polymarket intelligence crate inside the Poly-owned Calyx workspace. It\ningests public/read-only market evidence, stores it in local Calyx data structures, derives forecast\nsignals, grounds those signals against resolved outcomes, writes local forecast artifacts, and gates\nforecast admission. It does not place orders, sign orders, manage bankroll, use Polymarket trading\nsurfaces, or emit execution instructions.\n\n## Local Boundary\n\nAllowed work:\n\n- Read public market data and public on-chain data.\n- Persist local source snapshots, Calyx constellations, anchors, diagnostics, forecast artifacts,\n  policy decisions, admission rows, and score reports.\n- Launch forecast agents only through Infisical-backed runtime metadata and local artifact writeback.\n- Score forecasts against resolved outcomes with Brier, calibration, sufficiency, recall, and drift\n  evidence.\n\nForbidden work:\n\n- Any order signing, order submission, order cancellation, redemption, website trading, user-order\n  monitoring, bankroll management, stake sizing, Kelly sizing, or PnL optimization.\n- Any fallback that silently fabricates absent data, unresolved outcomes, uncalibrated guards, or\n  source provenance.\n\n## Core Flow\n\n1. Ingest: public/read-only snapshots enter `model`, `raw_sources`, or raw large-corpus helpers.\n2. Represent: `features`, `lenses`, `encode`, and `constellation` preserve typed numeric truth and\n   write Calyx slots/scalars without flattening.\n3. Associate: diagnostics and gates such as `panel_diagnostics`, `pair_gain_gate`, `kernel_recall`,\n   `kernel_recall_admission`, and `knn_base_rate` measure local association evidence.\n4. Ground: `grounding`, `outcome_backfill`, `anchor_floor`, `no_lookahead`, and\n   `resolved_market_corpus` bind evidence to resolved outcomes and refuse lookahead.\n5. Predict: `forecast`, `forecast_blend`, `forecast_calibration`, `forecast_ceiling`,\n   `calyx_native`, `oracle_forecast`, `ward_calibration`, and agent artifact modules create local\n   probability records.\n6. Gate: `admission`, `superiority`, `risk`, `oracle`, `wash`, `policy`, and `policy_audit` refuse\n   unsafe, stale, ungrounded, uncalibrated, or trading-related actions.\n7. Score: `score`, `backtest`, and `reproducibility` write durable local evidence for forecast\n   quality and bit-for-bit replay.\n\n## Module Map\n\n- `admission`: local forecast-quality gate; no execution economics.\n- `agent_artifacts`, `agent_launcher`, `agent_secrets`: optional DeepSeek forecast-agent artifacts\n  and Infisical-backed runtime metadata.\n- `book_liquidity`: read-only CLOB book-depth and liquidity feature rows.\n- `calyx_native`: local Calyx-native forecast record assembly.\n- `constellation`, `pipeline`: snapshot ingestion into Calyx slots, scalars, anchors, and vault rows.\n- `panel_sufficiency`, `panel_diagnostics`, `pair_gain_gate`: Assay/Loom-backed sufficiency and\n  interaction evidence.\n- `kernel_forecast`, `kernel_recall`, `kernel_recall_admission`, `knn_base_rate`: kernel and kNN\n  forecast evidence.\n- `oracle`, `oracle_forecast`, `risk`, `wash`: read-only data-quality and manipulation-risk screens.\n- `policy`, `policy_audit`: local-only runtime boundary and durable policy evidence.\n- `raw_sources`, `raw_large_corpus`, `schema_derivation`: public-source inventory, sampling, and\n  schema evidence.\n- `score`, `backtest`, `reproducibility`: outcome scoring, held-out validation, and artifact replay.\n- `ward_calibration`: Ward conformal calibration provenance for admission.\n\n## Build And Verification\n\nFrom `C:\\code\\poly\\Calyx`:\n\n```powershell\ncargo check -p calyx-poly\ncargo test -p calyx-poly\ncargo clippy -p calyx-poly -- -D warnings\n```\n\nProject doctrine treats those commands as supporting gates only. Full State Verification is the\nproof standard: execute the code, read back the source of truth separately, exercise at least three\nedges, and record the smallest corpus that fully proves the claim.\n\nOperational runbooks that are part of the crate's public verification surface live in\n`runbooks/`, with repository-level copies kept under `docs/` in the private development checkout.\n\n## FSV Pattern\n\nEvery non-trivial change should include:\n\n- Proof claim: the exact behavior being proven.\n- Minimum sufficient corpus: the smallest data set that proves the behavior, with why smaller is\n  insufficient and larger is wasteful.\n- Happy path: known-truth input with exact expected output.\n- At least three edges: stale, malformed, missing, insufficient, circular, ungrounded, uncalibrated,\n  crossed/invalid, or forbidden-action inputs as appropriate.\n- Source-of-truth readback: vault CF rows, files, graph artifacts, ledger entries, or issue state\n  read independently after execution.\n\n## Failure Policy\n\n`calyx-poly` fails closed. Unknown lens, missing source, non-finite numeric field, ungrounded\nevidence, stale calibration, insufficient anchors, malformed LLM output, forbidden action, or\nreadback mismatch must return a structured error and write no successful forecast/admission row.\n",

[L2]   "content": "<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/00-hero.jpg\" alt=\"ASTROLABE — Navigate any codebase by its constellations\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\n<h1 align=\"center\">ASTROLABE</h1>\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <b>The full-state-verification layer for AI coding agents.</b><br>\n  A single native MCP server that turns a repository into measured, grounded, distilled, guarded, predictive,\n  self-improving intelligence — with provenance for every claim, and a refusal wherever the evidence runs out.\n</p>\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <a href=\"#chapter-1--a-navigator-with-no-stars\">The story</a> ·\n  <a href=\"#the-tool-surface-40-tools\">40 tools</a> ·\n  <a href=\"#chapter-14--the-voyage-so-far\">Where it stands</a> ·\n  <a href=\"#build-it-yourself-windows\">Build it</a> ·\n  <a href=\"#read-these-next\">Read more</a>\n</p>\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img alt=\"Rust host\" src=\"https://img.shields.io/badge/host-Rust%201.95%20%C2%B7%20edition%202024-b7410e\">\n  <img alt=\"C engine\" src=\"https://img.shields.io/badge/engine-C%20%C2%B7%20libcbm.a-555\">\n  <img alt=\"MCP\" src=\"https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-40%20tools-1f6feb\">\n  <img alt=\"Languages\" src=\"https://img.shields.io/badge/parses-158%20languages-2ea043\">\n  <img alt=\"Target\" src=\"https://img.shields.io/badge/target-Windows%20native%20(x86__64--gnu)-0078d4\">\n  <img alt=\"State\" src=\"https://img.shields.io/badge/state%20of%20record-GitHub%20issues-8957e5\">\n</p>\n\n> **Status, honestly.** ASTROLABE is under heavy, active construction: **1,687 commits and 1,077 tracked issues since July 2026**, most of the intelligence stack live, and the flagship tool still ahead. It is Windows-only by design until the whole system works, it ships no release yet, and it has no test suite by owner directive — every claim below is verified by hand against real bytes on disk. Live project state lives **only** in [GitHub issues](https://github.com/ChrisRoyse/Astrolabe/issues); this README is the story, [EPIC #65](https://github.com/ChrisRoyse/Astrolabe/issues/65) is the truth.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 1 — A navigator with no stars\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/01-problem.jpg\" alt=\"An AI agent adrift on a sea of text with no stars to steer by\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nEvery AI coding agent today works from **text**. It greps. It reads a file. It infers structure from whatever it happened to open. Its context is a sample, its confidence is uncalibrated, and it has no memory of what was true last week or what actually broke last time.\n\nEven the best open-source code-graph servers — and [codebase-memory-mcp](cbm/) is the best decomposer in the open-source world — stop at the graph. They know *that* `f` calls `g`. They do not know whether that fact ever **mattered**: whether a test ever failed because of it, whether an incident ever traced through it, whether an agent's last change there was reverted. Their weights are hand-set constants, identical for a Haskell compiler and a React storefront. Their thresholds are fixed. Nothing is grounded, nothing is validated, and the system is exactly as smart on day 400 as on day 1.\n\nAn agent steering by that graph is a navigator with a map and no stars.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 2 — Two halves of one instrument\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/02-two-halves.jpg\" alt=\"codebase-memory-mcp and Calyx as two halves of one astrolabe\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nASTROLABE begins with an observation: two mature codebases, written independently, are each the missing half of the other.\n\n| | **codebase-memory-mcp** (`cbm/`) | **Calyx** (`calyx/`) |\n|---|---|---|\n| Language | C — ~120K lines of engine source, single static binary | Rust — ~557K lines across 24 crates |\n| What it does | **Decomposes** a repository into atoms and **associates** them: tree-sitter across **158 languages**, a hybrid type-aware LSP reverse-engineered from nine real language servers, **40+ typed edge types** (`CALLS`, `DATA_FLOWS`, `TESTS`, `HTTP_CALLS`, `EMITS`, `CROSS_*`, …), git context, watcher, incremental indexing, a 14-tool MCP surface | An **association-native database and grounded-intelligence engine**: an LSM vault with MVCC time-travel, cross-terms and reactive triggers, mutual-information measurement in bits, kernel distillation, a per-slot conformal guard, a prediction oracle, a hash-chained provenance ledger, and a reversible self-optimizer |\n| What it lacks | An intelligence layer: every weight guessed, nothing grounded, nothing improves | A code-domain front end: no parser, no graph extractor, no agent surface |\n\nNeither needed to be rewritten. Both were pulled into this repository **once**, and are now owned, first-class ASTROLABE source — edited directly, evolved in place. There are no pins, no patch overlays, no upstream tracking. The origin repos are, at most, a quarry.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 3 — The method\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/03-method.jpg\" alt=\"Decompose, Associate, Differentiate, Compose\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nCalyx's builder's handbook ([`docs/BUILDING_ON_CALYX.md`](docs/BUILDING_ON_CALYX.md)) has one foundational rule: *atoms → all base associations → differentiate → kernel → compose; never shortcut it.* CBM already performs the first two steps for the code domain more completely than any hand-built ingestion pipeline in any domain. Calyx is the engine for the last two.\n\n```\ncodebase-memory-mcp                          Calyx\n──────────────────────                       ─────────────────────────\n① DECOMPOSE  158-lang tree-sitter      →     measure: every symbol becomes a\n             + hybrid LSP → symbols          constellation through a lens panel\n② ASSOCIATE  40+ edge types,           →     count: cross-terms, agreement graph\n             cross-service, cross-repo,      ③ DIFFERENTIATE  bits, sufficiency,\n             git co-change, similarity          redundancy, synergy, causality\n                                             ④ COMPOSE  kernel, guard, oracle,\n                                                ledger, anneal, fused search\n```\n\n> **The thesis in one line:** CBM turns a repository into atoms and associations. Calyx turns atoms and associations into intelligence. Wire the output of the first into the input of the second, ground the result in real developer outcomes, and the loop closes — an MCP that gets measurably smarter about *your* codebase every day it is used.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 4 — Every symbol becomes a constellation\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/04-constellation.jpg\" alt=\"A code symbol measured through a ring of 24 lenses\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nThe astrolabe is the instrument for navigating by constellations. In ASTROLABE, the atomic record *is* a constellation: every function, class, struct, route, channel and module that CBM extracts is measured through a **panel of ~24 frozen lenses** (`S0`–`S22`) built almost entirely from signals CBM already computes — AST profiles, complexity, MinHash structure, API/type/decorator signatures, error surfaces, git temporal data, graph position — plus a small set of learned embeddings kept strictly separate from the deterministic encoders.\n\nTwo identities hold it all together ([`crates/astrolabe-domain`](crates/astrolabe-domain)):\n\n- a **series identity** — the qualified name, stable across versions, and\n- a **version identity** (`CxId`) — the content address of *(project, qualified name, canonical source bytes)*, so the same code always yields the same id and a changed byte always yields a new one.\n\nLens contracts are **frozen**: a lens that changes its shape is a new lens, never a silent edit, so measurements remain comparable across months of history. Anything that tries to violate that is refused with `CALYX_LENS_FROZEN_VIOLATION`.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 5 — Grounding\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/05-anchors.jpg\" alt=\"Constellations anchored to the seabed by tests, CI runs, traces, git history and agent outcomes\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nA graph without outcomes is opinion. ASTROLABE attaches **anchors** — real-world outcomes — to real symbols:\n\n| Anchor source | Tool | Trust |\n|---|---|---|\n| Test-suite reports (`junit_xml`, `cargo_test_json`, `pytest_verbose`, `go_test_json`, `vitest_json`) | `anchor_outcome` | `ci:` sources are **Trusted** (confidence exactly 1.0) |\n| Coverage reports (`lcov`, `coverage_py_json`, `cobertura_xml`) mapped line-exact to symbols | `coverage_ingest` | resolved, 1.0; one-hop `TESTS` propagation is proxy, 0.6 |\n| Runtime traces (OTLP protobuf / JSON) — production calls promote matching edges to Trusted and flag 5xx incidents | `ingest_traces` | Trusted |\n| Git archaeology — SZZ bug-introducing commits, reverts, fix commits | automatic on shadow index | `git:revert:` Trusted; `git:fix:` Provisional |\n| AI-agent task outcomes — the flywheel's own feedback | `anchor_outcome` with `agent:` | Provisional |\n\nThe trust of an anchor is decided by its source prefix and is **not negotiable**. Every anchor is written to the ledger, and every erasure (`anchor_erase`) is a tombstone plus a ledger entry — append-only physically, destructive to the serving view.\n\nThis is the difference between \"these two functions look related\" and \"these two functions have actually broken together before.\"\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 6 — Assay: bits, not guesses\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/06-assay.jpg\" alt=\"A balance scale weighing guessed constants against measured bits\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nCBM's original intelligence layer had an 11-signal semantic score with hand-set weights, fixed thresholds at 0.75 and 0.95, and edge confidences pinned at 0.5 / 0.55 / 0.75 / 0.90 / 0.95 — none measured against anything real, two of the eleven signals dead code.\n\nASTROLABE's **Assay** ([`crates/astrolabe-assay`](crates/astrolabe-assay), on Calyx's KSG mutual-information estimators) replaces every one of those with a per-repository **measurement in bits**, exposed through `measure_bits`:\n\n- `signals` — bits per lens slot about a real outcome axis, with confidence intervals\n- `sufficiency` — *I(panel; axis)* against *H(axis)*: literally \"how much of this outcome can our measurements explain, and what is missing\"\n- `redundancy` — total correlation, effective rank, pairwise map\n- `synergy` — three-way interaction information\n- `causality` — transfer-entropy `DRIVES` edges with lag sweep\n- `calibration` — each edge-resolution strategy's measured precision versus its prior, with Wilson intervals\n\n`assay_gate` then admits, parks or retires candidate lenses from those cards — ledgered and **reversible** byte-for-byte. The standing invariant behind all of it: **no constant that could be a measurement.**\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 7 — The Kernel\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/07-kernel.jpg\" alt=\"A galaxy of symbols with a small blazing core — the kernel\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nMost of a codebase is explained by a small part of it. The **kernel** ([`crates/astrolabe-kernel`](crates/astrolabe-kernel)) is that part, found rather than guessed: a deterministic full-graph feedback-vertex-set selection with a residual-DAG proof, a complete member index, and a **recall gate** — the kernel must meet an explicitly declared recall threshold (the blueprint's target is ≥ 0.95) against a corpus of real external queries before it is allowed to serve. The threshold is a required admission parameter, not a hidden constant.\n\n- `get_kernel` — build, read, and audit one atomically selected kernel generation; grounding-gap reports name the unanchored regions\n- `kernel_answer` — grounded Q&A: resolve an anchored entry point, walk association edges outward with `hop_score = edge_weight × 0.9^hop`, every hop carrying its ledger reference; refuse with a per-lens deficit rather than answer ungrounded\n\nThe kernel is the context engine. The flagship product built on it — a token-budgeted, recall-gated, reproducible **context pack** — is the one big piece still ahead (Chapter 16).\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 8 — The Guard\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/08-guard.jpg\" alt=\"A lighthouse sorting incoming code into accept, new region, quarantine and refuse\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nBefore agent-written code lands, the **Guard** ([`crates/astrolabe-guard`](crates/astrolabe-guard), on Calyx's conformal Ward) asks one question: *does this look like the code that works here?*\n\nIt measures the candidate on **the same instruments as indexing**, compares it per-slot against kernel-near trusted exemplars (`code_semantic`, `struct_trigrams`, `api_callees`, `name_semantic`, `complexity_profile`, `error_surface`, `public_api_signature`), and combines the per-slot verdicts — never a flattened average — into **`accept` / `new_region` / `quarantine` / `refuse`**, at a calibrated false-accept rate.\n\nThe calibration corpus builds itself: `guard_calibrate mode:\"generated\"` mutates real HEAD source, mines revert records, and borrows alien constellations from other indexed projects, enforcing a mix policy (≥ 50 bad cases, ≥ 3 generators, ≤ 60 % per generator) and failing closed on an under-mixed corpus. No hand-labelled data.\n\n`guard_lock` identity-locks a public API so breaking changes to it refuse; `guard_commit_ood` scores a whole commit; `guard_advisory_hook` is the 300 ms never-blocking fast path for editor hooks.\n\n> What the guard is not: it measures *distributional conformance to trusted exemplars*. It tells you \"this does not look like the code that works here.\" It does not tell you the code is correct — that is what the verification loop (Chapter 12) is for.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 9 — The Oracle\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/09-oracle.jpg\" alt=\"A compass rose with consequences rippling outward from one changed symbol\" width=\"100%\">\n</p>\n\nCBM's old `detect_changes` mapped hop-distance to risk: one hop away meant CRITICAL. That is topology, not evidence. The **Oracle** ([`crates/astrolabe-oracle`](crates/astrolabe-oracle)) grounds prediction in observed change→outcome history:\n\n| Question | Tool | How it answers |\n|---|---|---|\n| *If I change X, what breaks?* | `predict_impact` | cycle-guarded butterfly walk over real edges (×0.7 per hop, prune < 0.05, depth ≤ 4), three independent ceilings keeping probability strictly below 1.0; consequences crossing `TESTS` edges become a **ranked test-selection set** |\n| *This failed — what most plausibly caused it?* | `abduce_cause` | the same walk backwards; structural-only candidates capped at 0.35 and labelled provisional; every hypothesis names its **disconfirming test** |\n| *When will this flaky test bite again?* | `forecast` | median inter-arrival, credible interval, overdue hazard, CUSUM regime changes; refuses on self-inconsistent evidence |\n| *Is the system ready for questions about this scope?* | `get_readiness` | a six-tier predicate that fails closed per tier |\n| *What are the identifiable causal effects here?* | `causal_analysis`, `expected_gain` | persisted identifiable effects and expected net gains |\n\nAnd the honesty gate over all of it: a question the panel cannot support is **refused with a deficit**, never answered with a confident guess.\n\n---\n\n## Chapter 10 — Provenance\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"docs/readme-assets/... [L2]   "content": "---\nlicense: apache-2.0\nlibrary_name: transformers\npipeline_tag: text-classification\ntags: [laya, system-one, calibrated-decisions, rlcd, classification, routing, scoring, guardrails, moderation, reinforcement-learning, commercial-use]\n---\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"assets/logo-lockup.png\" alt=\"Laya\" width=\"330\" />\n</p>\n\n**Multilingual, non-autoregressive System 1 decision model.** Give it a **state** (text, email,\nticket, or JSON) and **typed questions**; it returns typed answers with probabilities in a\nsingle forward pass — 33 ms — across 100+ languages. Trained with reinforcement learning against\nstrictly proper scoring rules (**RLCD**), so reporting honest probabilities is the only way to\nmaximise reward. It never generates text, so there is nothing to parse and nothing to\nhallucinate.\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"assets/laya_vs_jev_full.png\" alt=\"Laya versus TypeSafe Jev: accuracy, every application workflow, all 51 languages, speed, calibration and routing cost\" width=\"100%\" />\n</p>\n\n**This repo holds all three checkpoints** and is the hub for the family. The English checkpoint\nis at the repo root; the other two are subfolders, and only the one you ask for is downloaded:\n\n```python\nimport laya\n\nlaya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\")                            # English\nlaya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\", subfolder=\"multilingual\")  # 100+ languages\nlaya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\", subfolder=\"typed-decisions\")\n```\n\n| checkpoint | encoder | params | context | use it for |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **`convaiinnovations/laya`** (this repo) | ModernBERT-large | 421M | 512 | English |\n| [`convaiinnovations/laya-multilingual`](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya-multilingual) | mmBERT-base | 322M | 1024 | 100+ languages, ~2x faster |\n| [`convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions`](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions) | ModernBERT-large | 421M | 1024 | the typed-decisions workflows |\n\n| question type | returns |\n|---|---|\n| `choice` | selected option, probability per option, confidence |\n| `score` | expected level on your ordinal rubric, distribution, confidence |\n| `noul` | calibrated probability P(true) |\n\n## Quickstart\n\n```bash\npip install laya\n```\n\n```python\nimport laya\n\nagent = laya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\")\nresult = agent.predict(\n    {\"subject\": \"Duplicate charge on invoice 4411\",\n     \"body\": \"We were billed twice for March. Please refund the duplicate.\"},\n    {\"department\": {\"type\": \"choice\", \"instructions\": \"Which team should handle this?\",\n                    \"criteria\": {\"billing\": \"invoices, payments, refunds\",\n                                 \"technical\": \"bugs and outages\", \"sales\": \"pricing\"}},\n     \"urgency\": {\"type\": \"score\", \"instructions\": \"How urgent is this?\",\n                 \"criteria\": [\"not urgent\", \"soon\", \"blocking\"]},\n     \"churn_risk\": {\"type\": \"noul\", \"instructions\": \"Does the user threaten to cancel?\"}},\n)\nprint(result[\"answers\"][\"department\"][\"choice\"])\n```\n\n### Routing between the three checkpoints\n\n```python\nfrom laya import Router\n\nrouter = Router()                       # lazy-loads only what a request needs\nrouter.predict({\"body\": \"I was charged twice\"}, questions)          # -> laya\nrouter.predict({\"body\": \"मुझसे दो बार शुल्क लिया गया\"}, questions)   # -> laya-multilingual\nrouter.predict(state, questions, model=\"typed-decisions\")           # explicit\n```\n\n**Preload for a server or a demo.** A cold checkpoint build costs seconds; detection costs\nmicroseconds. At the default `max_loaded=1`, alternating languages rebuilds a model on every\nrequest — measured at a 7.4 s median on CPU and 10.3 s on a T4.\n\n```python\nrouter = Router(preload=True)                # every checkpoint resident, routing is free\nrouter.attach(\"english\", existing_agent)     # reuse one you already built\n```\n\nOn a mixed workload this is worth up to **4.8×** at 50% non-English traffic.\n\n> **If `laya.load()` hangs:** `transformers` probes for TensorFlow at import, and when TF is\n> installed its abseil runtime can deadlock model construction. Run with `USE_TF=0`.\n\n## Architecture\n\n- **Backbone** ModernBERT-large (395M, bidirectional, fully fine-tuned) + a decision head\n  trained from scratch: 2 transformer layers, an option-marker scorer, and an act/escalate head.\n  421M total.\n- **Option markers** every option is scored at its own `[MASK]` token, then softmaxed over that\n  question's options. The answer space is defined at request time, so new schemas need no\n  retraining.\n- **Budget** 512 tokens per question (question + options + state).\n- **Batching** every question in a call is answered in one forward pass.\n\n## Training\n\n**RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions).** The policy reports a distribution;\nexploration adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to the logits; the reward is a strictly proper scoring\nrule (log + spherical, plus ranked probability score for ordinal questions). Expected reward is\nmaximised only by reporting honest probabilities. Updates are REINFORCE with a group-mean\nbaseline (GRPO-style). Multi-turn conversations use TD(λ=1.0) over prefix slices.\n\n7,313 updates, 1 epoch, ~1.96 h. Fitted temperatures `[1.637, 1.251, 1.983]` with\nper-option-count scaling.\n\n## Benchmarks\n\nMeasured on a Tesla T4; every checkpoint answered byte-identical questions in the same run.\n\n### Speed\n\n| questions/call | `laya` | `laya-multilingual` |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 | 39.5 ms | **32.8 ms** |\n| 10 | 158.6 ms (15.9 ms/q) | **72.3 ms (7.2 ms/q)** |\n| 50 | 771 ms | **337 ms (6.8 ms/q)** |\n\n103–332 questions/sec batched. TypeSafe Jev has been independently measured at 236–276 ms p50\n([AbdelStark](https://github.com/AbdelStark/jev-benchmarks),\n[nibzard](https://github.com/nibzard/decision-model-benchmark)), so Laya answers a single\nquestion roughly **6–7× faster**.\n\n### Laya (with routing) vs Jev\n\nEvery Laya figure is what `Router().predict(...)` returns — the checkpoint the router selects\nfor that input. Jev figures are **third-party published, never measured here** (no TypeSafe API\naccess); sample sizes and prompts differ.\n\n| | Jev 1.13.0 | Laya (routed) | |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| typed-decisions, 2,000 decisions | 0.727 | **0.766** | +0.039 |\n| AG News, 4 labels | 0.910 | **0.950** | +0.040 |\n| DAIR Emotion, 6 labels | 0.480 | **0.595** | +0.115 |\n| ECE *(lower better)* | 0.246 | **0.081** | 3× better |\n| p50 latency, 1 question | 236–276 ms | **32.8 ms** | 7.8× faster |\n| Languages usable | *no published benchmark* | **45 of 51** | — |\n| Weights | closed API | **Apache 2.0** | — |\n| Cost | $0.042 / 1M tokens | **$0 self-hosted** | — |\n\nOn DAIR Emotion, Jev assigned zero probability to the true label on 16% of examples.\n\nFull detail — every workflow, all 51 languages:\n[BENCHMARKS.md](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)\n\n### typed-decisions, all three checkpoints\n\n400 cases, 2,000 decisions, four workflows — measured here.\n\n| model | accuracy | soft acc | Brier | ECE | score MAE |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **`laya-typed-decisions`** | **0.766** | 0.471 | **0.062** | 0.213 | **0.242** |\n| `laya` | 0.362 | 0.332 | 0.316 | 0.175 | 0.694 |\n| `laya-multilingual` | 0.342 | 0.326 | 0.439 | 0.285 | 0.687 |\n| *Jev 1.13.0 (published)* | *0.727* | *0.580* | *0.148* | *0.144* | *0.391* |\n| *teacher ceiling* | *0.735* | | | | |\n| *majority class* | *0.461* | | | | |\n\nThe fine-tuned checkpoint clears the teacher ceiling and wins all four workflows: invoice\nprocessing 0.804, security incidents 0.766, customer service 0.764, agent-trace observability\n0.730. By primitive: `noul` 0.857, `choice` 0.733, `score` 0.723.\n\nThe base checkpoints sit below the majority-class baseline here — the capability on this\nbenchmark comes from fine-tuning, which is what the\n[fine-tuning notebook](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya/blob/main/notebooks/laya_finetune_typed_decisions_2xT4_kaggle.ipynb)\nis for.\n\n### English tasks\n\n| task | `laya` | `laya-multilingual` | |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| AG News | **0.947** | 0.937 | in training mix |\n| BoolQ | **0.830** | 0.787 | in training mix |\n| DAIR Emotion | **0.573** | 0.513 | held out |\n| prompt-injections | **0.698** | 0.578 | held out, n=116 |\n| SST-5 (ordinal) | 0.372 | 0.282 | held out |\n\n### Languages — use `laya-multilingual` outside English\n\nAcross 51 languages on MASSIVE intent (20 options, random = 0.050), this checkpoint\nmacro-averages **0.227** with macro ECE **0.733**, clearing 3× random on only 23 of 51.\nKhmer scores **0.000 accuracy at 0.952 confidence**.\n\n| | `laya` | `laya-multilingual` |\n|---|---|---|\n| MASSIVE intent, English | **0.783** | 0.657 |\n| MASSIVE intent, 13 others | 0.306 | **0.451** |\n| XNLI, English | **0.860** | 0.843 |\n| XNLI, 14 others | 0.521 | **0.731** |\n\nThe confidence score gives no warning when the input is unreadable, so the choice has to be made\nbefore the forward pass — that is what `Router` is for.\n\n## Limits\n\n- **Near chance on typed-decisions zero-shot** — 0.362 here and 0.352 for multilingual, against a\n  0.318 random and 0.461 majority-class baseline. The 0.766 belongs to the checkpoint fine-tuned\n  on that benchmark's own training split. Laya is a fast base to specialise, not a zero-shot\n  decision engine.\n- **Keep `choice` questions under ~20 options.** Options share a fixed `head_max_len` budget\n  (192 tokens here), so a very large label space leaves only a few tokens per label and\n  accuracy falls off sharply. Split into a coarse choice then a fine one.\n- Ordinal `score` questions are the weakest primitive (SST-5 0.372).\n- Ships over-confident: refitting one temperature per (question type, option count) moves mean\n  ECE **0.466 → 0.081**. Do this on your own data before trusting the probabilities.\n- English only. Use `laya-multilingual` for anything else.\n\n## Links\n\n- **GitHub** https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya\n- **PyPI** https://pypi.org/project/laya/\n- **Demo** https://huggingface.co/spaces/convaiinnovations/laya-demo\n- **Write-up** [dev.to](https://dev.to/nandakishor_m_6cc0adfde9f/i-built-non-autoregressive-decision-models-a-year-ago-then-a-frontier-lab-called-it-a-18me)\n\nApache 2.0 · Convai Innovations\n",

[L2]   "content": "//! Domain×horizon calibration slope: fit + de-bias (issue #86).\n//!\n//! Raw model probabilities and raw market prices are systematically miscalibrated per domain and\n//! horizon (politics is chronically under-confident; short-horizon crypto over-reacts). This module\n//! fits a **Platt scaling** slope `p_cal = σ(a + b·logit(p_raw))` on resolved `(p_raw, outcome)`\n//! history for one `(domain, horizon)` bucket, then applies it to de-bias both `p_model` and the\n//! market price. The fit is deterministic gradient descent on logistic loss (fixed init `a=0, b=1`,\n//! fixed iteration count) so the slope is reproducible. Fail closed below the sample floor or on a\n//! single-class history (a slope needs both outcomes) or non-finite input.\n\nuse serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};\n\nuse crate::error::{PolyError, Result};\nuse crate::forecast::{logit, sigmoid};\n\n/// Minimum resolved samples to fit a calibration slope.\npub const MIN_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES: usize = 30;\n/// Gradient-descent iterations (fixed for reproducibility).\npub const CALIBRATION_ITERS: usize = 2000;\n/// Gradient-descent learning rate.\npub const CALIBRATION_LR: f64 = 0.05;\n\n/// Too few resolved samples to fit a slope.\npub const ERR_CAL_SAMPLES: &str = \"CALYX_POLY_CALIBRATION_INSUFFICIENT_SAMPLES\";\n/// The resolved history is single-class (all YES or all NO) — no slope is identifiable.\npub const ERR_CAL_SINGLE_CLASS: &str = \"CALYX_POLY_CALIBRATION_SINGLE_CLASS\";\n/// A probability in the history was not finite in `[0, 1]`.\npub const ERR_CAL_PROBABILITY: &str = \"CALYX_POLY_CALIBRATION_PROBABILITY\";\n\n/// Horizon buckets by seconds-to-resolution.\npub fn horizon_bucket(secs_to_resolution: f64) -> &'static str {\n    if !secs_to_resolution.is_finite() || secs_to_resolution < 0.0 {\n        \"unknown\"\n    } else if secs_to_resolution < 3_600.0 {\n        \"lt_1h\"\n    } else if secs_to_resolution < 86_400.0 {\n        \"1h_24h\"\n    } else if secs_to_resolution < 7.0 * 86_400.0 {\n        \"1d_7d\"\n    } else {\n        \"gt_7d\"\n    }\n}\n\n/// A fitted per-(domain, horizon) calibration slope with in-sample Brier before/after.\n#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]\npub struct CalibrationSlope {\n    /// Domain slug.\n    pub domain: String,\n    /// Horizon bucket.\n    pub horizon_bucket: String,\n    /// Platt intercept.\n    pub a: f64,\n    /// Platt slope on the raw logit.\n    pub b: f64,\n    /// Resolved samples fit.\n    pub n: usize,\n    /// In-sample Brier score of the raw probabilities.\n    pub brier_raw: f64,\n    /// In-sample Brier score after calibration.\n    pub brier_calibrated: f64,\n}\n\n/// Fits a calibration slope on resolved `(p_raw, outcome)` pairs for one `(domain, horizon)` bucket.\npub fn fit_calibration_slope(\n    domain: &str,\n    horizon_bucket: &str,\n    pairs: &[(f64, bool)],\n) -> Result<CalibrationSlope> {\n    if pairs.len() < MIN_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES {\n        return Err(PolyError::diagnostics(\n            ERR_CAL_SAMPLES,\n            format!(\n                \"calibration for {domain}/{horizon_bucket} needs >= {MIN_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES} resolved samples, got {}\",\n                pairs.len()\n            ),\n        ));\n    }\n    let positives = pairs.iter().filter(|(_, y)| *y).count();\n    if positives == 0 || positives == pairs.len() {\n        return Err(PolyError::diagnostics(\n            ERR_CAL_SINGLE_CLASS,\n            format!(\n                \"calibration for {domain}/{horizon_bucket} history is single-class ({positives} of {} YES)\",\n                pairs.len()\n            ),\n        ));\n    }\n    let mut features = Vec::with_capacity(pairs.len());\n    for (p, y) in pairs {\n        if !p.is_finite() || !(0.0..=1.0).contains(p) {\n            return Err(PolyError::diagnostics(\n                ERR_CAL_PROBABILITY,\n                format!(\"calibration history probability {p} must be finite in [0, 1]\"),\n            ));\n        }\n        features.push((logit(*p), if *y { 1.0 } else { 0.0 }));\n    }\n\n    // Deterministic gradient descent on logistic loss over p_cal = sigmoid(a + b*x).\n    let (mut a, mut b) = (0.0f64, 1.0f64);\n    let n = features.len() as f64;\n    for _ in 0..CALIBRATION_ITERS {\n        let (mut grad_a, mut grad_b) = (0.0, 0.0);\n        for (x, y) in &features {\n            let pred = sigmoid(a + b * x);\n            let err = pred - y;\n            grad_a += err;\n            grad_b += err * x;\n        }\n        a -= CALIBRATION_LR * grad_a / n;\n        b -= CALIBRATION_LR * grad_b / n;\n    }\n\n    let slope = CalibrationSlope {\n        domain: domain.to_string(),\n        horizon_bucket: horizon_bucket.to_string(),\n        a,\n        b,\n        n: pairs.len(),\n        brier_raw: brier(pairs.iter().map(|(p, y)| (*p, *y))),\n        brier_calibrated: brier(pairs.iter().map(|(p, y)| (apply_slope(a, b, *p), *y))),\n    };\n    Ok(slope)\n}\n\n/// Applies a fitted slope to de-bias a raw probability (a `p_model` or a market price).\npub fn apply_calibration(slope: &CalibrationSlope, p_raw: f64) -> f64 {\n    apply_slope(slope.a, slope.b, p_raw)\n}\n\nfn apply_slope(a: f64, b: f64, p_raw: f64) -> f64 {\n    sigmoid(a + b * logit(p_raw.clamp(0.0, 1.0)))\n}\n\nfn brier(pairs: impl Iterator<Item = (f64, bool)>) -> f64 {\n    let mut sum = 0.0;\n    let mut n = 0.0;\n    for (p, y) in pairs {\n        let target = if y { 1.0 } else { 0.0 };\n        sum += (p - target).powi(2);\n        n += 1.0;\n    }\n    if n > 0.0 { sum / n } else { 0.0 }\n}\n\n#[cfg(test)]\nmod tests {\n    use super::*;\n\n    #[test]\n    fn horizon_buckets_partition() {\n        assert_eq!(horizon_bucket(600.0), \"lt_1h\");\n        assert_eq!(horizon_bucket(3_600.0), \"1h_24h\");\n        assert_eq!(horizon_bucket(200_000.0), \"1d_7d\");\n        assert_eq!(horizon_bucket(1_000_000.0), \"gt_7d\");\n        assert_eq!(horizon_bucket(-1.0), \"unknown\");\n    }\n\n    #[test]\n    fn underconfident_history_is_corrected() {\n        // Construct an under-confident forecaster: it says 0.6 when the truth resolves YES 80% of the\n        // time, and 0.4 when YES 20% of the time. Calibration should stretch probabilities outward\n        // and lower the Brier score.\n        let mut pairs = Vec::new();\n        for i in 0..100 {\n            // p=0.6 group, 80% YES\n            pairs.push((0.6, i % 5 != 0));\n            // p=0.4 group, 20% YES\n            pairs.push((0.4, i % 5 == 0));\n        }\n        let slope = fit_calibration_slope(\"crypto\", \"1h_24h\", &pairs).unwrap();\n        assert!(\n            slope.b > 1.0,\n            \"under-confidence must be stretched (b>1): b={}\",\n            slope.b\n        );\n        assert!(\n            slope.brier_calibrated < slope.brier_raw,\n            \"calibration must lower Brier: {} -> {}\",\n            slope.brier_raw,\n            slope.brier_calibrated\n        );\n        // 0.6 raw should move up toward 0.8.\n        let cal = apply_calibration(&slope, 0.6);\n        assert!(cal > 0.6, \"0.6 should be pushed up, got {cal}\");\n    }\n\n    #[test]\n    fn fails_closed_below_floor_and_single_class() {\n        assert_eq!(\n            fit_calibration_slope(\"d\", \"h\", &[(0.5, true); 10])\n                .unwrap_err()\n                .code(),\n            ERR_CAL_SAMPLES\n        );\n        assert_eq!(\n            fit_calibration_slope(\"d\", \"h\", &[(0.5, true); 40])\n                .unwrap_err()\n                .code(),\n            ERR_CAL_SINGLE_CLASS\n        );\n    }\n}\n",

[L2]   "content": "---\nlicense: apache-2.0\nlibrary_name: transformers\npipeline_tag: text-classification\ntags: [laya, system-one, calibrated-decisions, rlcd, classification, routing, scoring, guardrails, moderation, reinforcement-learning, commercial-use]\n---\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"assets/logo-lockup.png\" alt=\"Laya\" width=\"330\" />\n</p>\n\n**Multilingual, non-autoregressive System 1 decision model.** Give it a **state** (text, email,\nticket, or JSON) and **typed questions**; it returns typed answers with probabilities in a\nsingle forward pass — 33 ms — across 100+ languages. Trained with reinforcement learning against\nstrictly proper scoring rules (**RLCD**), so reporting honest probabilities is the only way to\nmaximise reward. It never generates text, so there is nothing to parse and nothing to\nhallucinate.\n\n<p align=\"center\">\n  <img src=\"assets/laya_vs_jev_full.png\" alt=\"Laya versus TypeSafe Jev: accuracy, every application workflow, all 51 languages, speed, calibration and routing cost\" width=\"100%\" />\n</p>\n\n**This repo holds all three checkpoints** and is the hub for the family. The English checkpoint\nis at the repo root; the other two are subfolders, and only the one you ask for is downloaded:\n\n```python\nimport laya\n\nlaya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\")                            # English\nlaya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\", subfolder=\"multilingual\")  # 100+ languages\nlaya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\", subfolder=\"typed-decisions\")\n```\n\n| checkpoint | encoder | params | context | use it for |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **`convaiinnovations/laya`** (this repo) | ModernBERT-large | 421M | 512 | English |\n| [`convaiinnovations/laya-multilingual`](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya-multilingual) | mmBERT-base | 322M | 1024 | 100+ languages, ~2x faster |\n| [`convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions`](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions) | ModernBERT-large | 421M | 1024 | the typed-decisions workflows |\n\n| question type | returns |\n|---|---|\n| `choice` | selected option, probability per option, confidence |\n| `score` | expected level on your ordinal rubric, distribution, confidence |\n| `noul` | calibrated probability P(true) |\n\n## Quickstart\n\n```bash\npip install laya\n```\n\n```python\nimport laya\n\nagent = laya.load(\"convaiinnovations/laya\")\nresult = agent.predict(\n    {\"subject\": \"Duplicate charge on invoice 4411\",\n     \"body\": \"We were billed twice for March. Please refund the duplicate.\"},\n    {\"department\": {\"type\": \"choice\", \"instructions\": \"Which team should handle this?\",\n                    \"criteria\": {\"billing\": \"invoices, payments, refunds\",\n                                 \"technical\": \"bugs and outages\", \"sales\": \"pricing\"}},\n     \"urgency\": {\"type\": \"score\", \"instructions\": \"How urgent is this?\",\n                 \"criteria\": [\"not urgent\", \"soon\", \"blocking\"]},\n     \"churn_risk\": {\"type\": \"noul\", \"instructions\": \"Does the user threaten to cancel?\"}},\n)\nprint(result[\"answers\"][\"department\"][\"choice\"])\n```\n\n### Routing between the three checkpoints\n\n```python\nfrom laya import Router\n\nrouter = Router()                       # lazy-loads only what a request needs\nrouter.predict({\"body\": \"I was charged twice\"}, questions)          # -> laya\nrouter.predict({\"body\": \"मुझसे दो बार शुल्क लिया गया\"}, questions)   # -> laya-multilingual\nrouter.predict(state, questions, model=\"typed-decisions\")           # explicit\n```\n\n**Preload for a server or a demo.** A cold checkpoint build costs seconds; detection costs\nmicroseconds. At the default `max_loaded=1`, alternating languages rebuilds a model on every\nrequest — measured at a 7.4 s median on CPU and 10.3 s on a T4.\n\n```python\nrouter = Router(preload=True)                # every checkpoint resident, routing is free\nrouter.attach(\"english\", existing_agent)     # reuse one you already built\n```\n\nOn a mixed workload this is worth up to **4.8×** at 50% non-English traffic.\n\n> **If `laya.load()` hangs:** `transformers` probes for TensorFlow at import, and when TF is\n> installed its abseil runtime can deadlock model construction. Run with `USE_TF=0`.\n\n## Architecture\n\n- **Backbone** ModernBERT-large (395M, bidirectional, fully fine-tuned) + a decision head\n  trained from scratch: 2 transformer layers, an option-marker scorer, and an act/escalate head.\n  421M total.\n- **Option markers** every option is scored at its own `[MASK]` token, then softmaxed over that\n  question's options. The answer space is defined at request time, so new schemas need no\n  retraining.\n- **Budget** 512 tokens per question (question + options + state).\n- **Batching** every question in a call is answered in one forward pass.\n\n## Training\n\n**RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions).** The policy reports a distribution;\nexploration adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to the logits; the reward is a strictly proper scoring\nrule (log + spherical, plus ranked probability score for ordinal questions). Expected reward is\nmaximised only by reporting honest probabilities. Updates are REINFORCE with a group-mean\nbaseline (GRPO-style). Multi-turn conversations use TD(λ=1.0) over prefix slices.\n\n7,313 updates, 1 epoch, ~1.96 h. Fitted temperatures `[1.637, 1.251, 1.983]` with\nper-option-count scaling.\n\n## Benchmarks\n\nMeasured on a Tesla T4; every checkpoint answered byte-identical questions in the same run.\n\n### Speed\n\n| questions/call | `laya` | `laya-multilingual` |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 | 39.5 ms | **32.8 ms** |\n| 10 | 158.6 ms (15.9 ms/q) | **72.3 ms (7.2 ms/q)** |\n| 50 | 771 ms | **337 ms (6.8 ms/q)** |\n\n103–332 questions/sec batched. TypeSafe Jev has been independently measured at 236–276 ms p50\n([AbdelStark](https://github.com/AbdelStark/jev-benchmarks),\n[nibzard](https://github.com/nibzard/decision-model-benchmark)), so Laya answers a single\nquestion roughly **6–7× faster**.\n\n### Laya (with routing) vs Jev\n\nEvery Laya figure is what `Router().predict(...)` returns — the checkpoint the router selects\nfor that input. Jev figures are **third-party published, never measured here** (no TypeSafe API\naccess); sample sizes and prompts differ.\n\n| | Jev 1.13.0 | Laya (routed) | |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| typed-decisions, 2,000 decisions | 0.727 | **0.766** | +0.039 |\n| AG News, 4 labels | 0.910 | **0.950** | +0.040 |\n| DAIR Emotion, 6 labels | 0.480 | **0.595** | +0.115 |\n| ECE *(lower better)* | 0.246 | **0.081** | 3× better |\n| p50 latency, 1 question | 236–276 ms | **32.8 ms** | 7.8× faster |\n| Languages usable | *no published benchmark* | **45 of 51** | — |\n| Weights | closed API | **Apache 2.0** | — |\n| Cost | $0.042 / 1M tokens | **$0 self-hosted** | — |\n\nOn DAIR Emotion, Jev assigned zero probability to the true label on 16% of examples.\n\nFull detail — every workflow, all 51 languages:\n[BENCHMARKS.md](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)\n\n### typed-decisions, all three checkpoints\n\n400 cases, 2,000 decisions, four workflows — measured here.\n\n| model | accuracy | soft acc | Brier | ECE | score MAE |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **`laya-typed-decisions`** | **0.766** | 0.471 | **0.062** | 0.213 | **0.242** |\n| `laya` | 0.362 | 0.332 | 0.316 | 0.175 | 0.694 |\n| `laya-multilingual` | 0.342 | 0.326 | 0.439 | 0.285 | 0.687 |\n| *Jev 1.13.0 (published)* | *0.727* | *0.580* | *0.148* | *0.144* | *0.391* |\n| *teacher ceiling* | *0.735* | | | | |\n| *majority class* | *0.461* | | | | |\n\nThe fine-tuned checkpoint clears the teacher ceiling and wins all four workflows: invoice\nprocessing 0.804, security incidents 0.766, customer service 0.764, agent-trace observability\n0.730. By primitive: `noul` 0.857, `choice` 0.733, `score` 0.723.\n\nThe base checkpoints sit below the majority-class baseline here — the capability on this\nbenchmark comes from fine-tuning, which is what the\n[fine-tuning notebook](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya/blob/main/notebooks/laya_finetune_typed_decisions_2xT4_kaggle.ipynb)\nis for.\n\n### English tasks\n\n| task | `laya` | `laya-multilingual` | |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| AG News | **0.947** | 0.937 | in training mix |\n| BoolQ | **0.830** | 0.787 | in training mix |\n| DAIR Emotion | **0.573** | 0.513 | held out |\n| prompt-injections | **0.698** | 0.578 | held out, n=116 |\n| SST-5 (ordinal) | 0.372 | 0.282 | held out |\n\n### Languages — use `laya-multilingual` outside English\n\nAcross 51 languages on MASSIVE intent (20 options, random = 0.050), this checkpoint\nmacro-averages **0.227** with macro ECE **0.733**, clearing 3× random on only 23 of 51.\nKhmer scores **0.000 accuracy at 0.952 confidence**.\n\n| | `laya` | `laya-multilingual` |\n|---|---|---|\n| MASSIVE intent, English | **0.783** | 0.657 |\n| MASSIVE intent, 13 others | 0.306 | **0.451** |\n| XNLI, English | **0.860** | 0.843 |\n| XNLI, 14 others | 0.521 | **0.731** |\n\nThe confidence score gives no warning when the input is unreadable, so the choice has to be made\nbefore the forward pass — that is what `Router` is for.\n\n## Limits\n\n- **Near chance on typed-decisions zero-shot** — 0.362 here and 0.352 for multilingual, against a\n  0.318 random and 0.461 majority-class baseline. Laya is a fast base to specialise, not a zero-shot\n  decision engine.\n- **Keep `choice` questions under ~20 options.** Options share a fixed `head_max_len` budget\n  (192 tokens here), so a very large label space leaves only a few tokens per label and\n  accuracy falls off sharply. Do this on your own data before trusting the probabilities.\n- English only. In the application, only voice reaches\nthem: `withToolCatalog` in `src/voice/gevRealtime.js` imports the\nfunction-calling adapter, and the standalone entry supplies the catalog.\n\n## Definitions and composition\n\n`defineTool({ name, kind, title, description, inputSchema, requires, run })`\nvalidates and freezes a tool. `kind` is `query` (answers from data, read-only)\nor `action`. `inputSchema` uses a JSON Schema subset that `src/tools/schema.js`\nchecks completely; unsupported keywords are rejected at definition time.\n`run(args, { services, signal })` resolves to `{ summary, data }`: one sentence\nfor people and a structured object for programs. A tool may also return `images`,\neach `{ mimeType, data }` with base64 data; the MCP adapter sends them as image\ncontent. MCP results carry the summary and the data as JSON text, plus the data\nas `structuredContent`, for clients that read only one of them.\n\n`composeCatalog({ tools, services, replace, interceptors })` builds a catalog:\n\n- **Tools**: an application adds its own tools to `coreTools`. Reusing a name\n  fails unless the name is listed in `replace`.\n- **Services**: each tool names the services it reads in `requires`. Tools\n  whose services are not supplied are left out.\n- **Interceptors**: `(call, next) => next(call)` functions wrap every call,\n  outermost first. They can observe, reject or change a call.\n- **Composite tools**: `run` receives `tools`, with `has(name)` and\n  `call(name, args)`, to call other tools through the same catalog, so\n  replaced tools and interceptors apply. Interceptors see such calls with\n  `parent`, the calling tool's name.\n\n### Surfaces\n\n`src/tools/surfaces.js` lists which tools MCP and voice offer. A tool is on\nboth unless `TOOL_SURFACES` turns it off; edit an entry to turn a tool on or\noff for one surface. MCP leaves out place search, routing, plain\nweather and wind, the regional brief, the HUD caption, radio, bike share and\ntransit, which assistants already cover or which add little without the\nglobe. `catalogForSurface(catalog, surface, overrides)` is the\nview a surface exposes: it lists and calls only the tools it offers, while\ncomposite tools still reach the whole catalog. `toolsForSurface` gives the\nsame selection as a list of definitions, such as for the voice session's tool\nlist. Voice leaves out tools that answer with images, link to the app, or\nrepeat what its app actions answer.\n\nExpected failures throw `ToolError` with one of `invalid_arguments`,\n`unavailable`, `unsupported`, `malformed` or `retry_later`. Other errors are\nreported to clients without details.\n\n## Services\n\n`gods-eye-view/tools/services` builds the default set with\n`createToolServices({ fetchImpl, appUrl })`. Services are the portable source factories the layers already use, such as\n`createUsgsEarthquakeSource`, `createFirmsSource` and `createLaunchSource`,\nplus a `places` service with `resolve(name, { signal })`. Sources request\nrelative `/api/...` paths through an injected `fetchImpl`, so the same tool\ncode runs wherever an application routes those paths.\nThe `weather`, `regional`, `terrain`, `summary` and `features` services are the\napplication request services from `gods-eye-view/application/requests`.\n`situation_brief` and `military_awareness` run each section whose services are supplied and mark the\nothers unavailable. `app` is `{ baseUrl }`, the address links open. The `bikeshare` service is `{ systems, getStations }`: the system registry and\nthe GBFS source. `createGeocodePlaceService` resolves place names through `/api/geocode`;\n`createPlaceSearchService` searches `/api/google/*` and reports when no search key\nis configured; `createRouteService` plans routes through `/api/route`.\n\n## Views\n\n`gods-eye-view/view` (`src/view/index.js`) describes what the app shows,\nindependent of how it is shown: a camera (lat, lon, altitude, heading,\npitch), data layers, visual style, map imagery, and an aircraft, military\naircraft or satellite to follow. `createView` builds and bounds one,\n`viewToParams` and `viewFromParams` write and read it in the share-link\nformat the app restores, and `viewUrl` gives the address that opens it. The\nstyle names are the ones share links use. Ships cannot be followed from a\nlink yet. An aircraft's `follow` may ask for its cockpit view\n(`cockpit: true`); links cannot carry that and open the app following it.\n\nA view can also carry `annotations`, the marks the app's `annotate_map`\naction draws (pins, highlights, areas, arrows, routes and labels at a place\nname or coordinates). Links carry them in the `an` parameter, and the app\ndraws them once the link has been restored.\n\nTools take a view as `VIEW_ARGUMENTS`: an `area` to frame from above, or a\n`camera`, plus `layers`, `style`, `map`, `follow` and `annotations`. A\ntilted camera over an area looks at its center from behind; camera fields\ngiven with an area override its framing. `resolveViewArguments` turns them\ninto a view.\n\n### The God's Eye View panel\n\n`show_in_gods_eye_view` names an MCP Apps view (`io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`):\n`_meta.ui.resourceUri` is `ui://gods-eye-view/globe`, a `text/html;profile=mcp-app`\nresource from `createGlobePanelResource({ runtime })` in\n`src/tools/globePanel.js`, with the panel's script from\n`src/app/globePanelRuntime.js`. Clients that display apps render it inside\nthe conversation. The panel completes the MCP Apps handshake\n(`ui/initialize`, `ui/notifications/initialized`,\n`ui/notifications/size-changed`), and for each\n`ui/notifications/tool-result` carrying a view it loads the app in inline\nembed mode the first time and posts later views to that same app, so the\nglobe changes without reloading. Its \"Open in God's Eye View\" button asks\nthe host to open the link (`ui/open-link`).\n\nHosts serve panels from their own sites and may refuse other addresses;\nCodex, for one, refuses any address on the user's machine. So the panel\nnever requests the app's server itself. It loads everything from the app's\nown paths through `panel_request`, a tool meant for the panel: it is\nmarked `_meta.ui.visibility: [\"app\"]`, and each call must carry the key the\nMCP server puts in its panel page. Any client can read that page, so the key\nkeeps the tool from clients that only list it, and is not access control. The\nMCP server requests the path from the app's server and returns the response,\ncompressed and in parts when large.\nThe same path works in every host. Only\nmap imagery, tiles and fonts load directly, from the providers the\nresource's `csp` lists. `panel_request` refuses Provider Settings\n(`/api/setup`), credential and model endpoints (`/api/realtime`,\n`/api/openai`), `/mcp` and the development server's internal routes, in any\nletter case, encoding or dot suffix.\n\nThe panel loads the app's panel build, which `npm run build:panel` writes to\n`dist/panel` and the servers serve at `/panel/`: one app script, one\nstylesheet, and Cesium's script, which carries its workers and starts them\nfrom memory (`CESIUM_WORKERS`). Files those workers load themselves are\nembedded in a prelude the panel runs ahead of them, since a worker's\nrequests reach the panel page's own site. Rebuild it after changing\nthe app.\n\nHosts differ in ways the panel works around, all inside the panel only:\nimages and stylesheet files arrive as `data:` URLs, since some hosts refuse\n`blob:` images; code that needs an https address for the app gets\n`GEV_APP_BASE_URL`, since some hosts serve the page from their own scheme;\nthe globe keeps drawing from a timer when the host reports the panel hidden\nand stops animation frames; and 2D canvases are kept in memory\n(`willReadFrequently`), since a host that treats the panel as off screen may\ndrop their GPU contents and show the overlays as black over the globe.\n\nTools declare a UI resource with `defineTool({ ui: { resourceUri } })`, and\nan app-only tool with `ui: { visibility: ['app'] }`;\n`createMcpServer({ resources })` serves `resources/list` and\n`resources/read`.\n\n### Embed mode\n\n`?embed=1` shows only the globe: clean view, with the HUD, panels, welcome\nand setup prompts hidden; provider attribution stays. A page that frames it\nchanges the view by posting `{ type: 'gev:view', id, view }` to the frame.\nThe app applies it through its own actions (style, map, exactly the view's\nlayers, annotations, then the followed entity, retried until its layer has\nit, or the camera when nothing is followed or the entity is not there yet,\nsince a camera flight would end the follow; then cockpit view when asked) and\nanswers `{ type: 'gev:view-applied', id, ok, steps }` to the origin that\nsent the view. It posts `{ type: 'gev:ready' }` once it can take views, and\nonly its parent page can send them. See `src/app/embed.js`.\n\nNo page may frame the app by default: every document keeps\n`X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `frame-ancestors 'none'`. Setting\n`GEV_EMBED_FRAME_ANCESTORS` lets the pages it names (CSP frame-ancestors\nsources, or `*` for any page) frame embed-mode documents only. The MCP Apps\npanel loads the app into its own page and needs no framing.\n\nAnswers that have something to show include `data.view`: the view that\nshows them, with the matching layers on, an area framed from above, and a\nsingle aircraft or satellite followed, plus `url` to open it (null when the\napp's address is not configured). `suggestView` in `src/tools/views.js`\nbuilds one.\n\n## The `area` argument\n\nLocation-scoped tools take `area` as exactly one of a `place` name, a `bbox`\n(`[west, south, east, north]`, crossing the antimeridian when west exceeds\neast), or `lat`, `lon` and `radius_km`. Lists default to 25 rows, at most 200,\nand report `total`, `returned` and `truncated`.\n\n## MCP\n\n`createMcpServer({ catalog, name, version, instructions, descriptions, decorate })`\nimplements `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list` and `tools/call` for protocol\nrevisions 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26. `descriptions` overrides a\ntool's title or description for this surface; `decorate(definition, tool)`\nmerges extra fields into each listed definition. `createMcpHttpHandler(server)`\nreturns a `Request`-to-`Response` handler for stateless Streamable HTTP: one\nJSON-RPC message per POST, answered with JSON. The host owns routing and any\naccess control in front of it.\n\n## Voice\n\nVoice offers the catalog's queries next to its app actions.\n`toFunctionTools(tools, { exclude })` turns tools into\n`{ type: 'function', name, description, parameters }` records, and\n`toFunctionOutput(name, result)` turns a result into\n`{ ok, tool, summary, data }`, counting images in `images_omitted` instead of\nsending them.\n\nThe voice session token endpoint takes its tool list as `realtime.tools`.\n`realtimeSessionTools(additional)` appends function tools to the app actions,\nskipping names an action already uses, so `next_satellite_pass` stays the\naction. ## GEV integration — verified starting point

I located the actual packet in your ChatGPT Library:

**`08_GEV_OMP_Handoff.zip`**

There are two copies, and their SHA-256 hashes match exactly. The packet contains seven files, including the audited GEV deployment PRD v1.2, OMP instructions, and acceptance criteria.

The deployment specification identifies GEV as the existing GMRI macro-scale geospatial system, with a trusted-network service and a Radeon-driven kiosk on the iMac's built-in 5K display.

**I'm treating GEV as operational, as you've stated.** The packet describes its deployment and integration constraints; it isn't a live status report.

The important integration boundary is clear: new models can provide perception, reasoning, prediction, and voice without replacing GEV's existing renderer, data sources, or provenance model.

The engineering task is to extend the working system, not rebuild it.

## Two important model findings — October 28, 2026

### LFM3 was released yesterday

Liquid AI announced **LFM3 on October 27, 2026**, and it is unusually well aligned with your proposed LAYA combination.

<box gap={2}>
  <row align=start gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage query="Liquid AI LFM3 October 27 2026 model family audio omni decision launch graphic" aspectRatio="5:4" maxWidth="136px"/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **<Link url="https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm3" title="LFM3 official launch"/>**

      Six related models, including speech, vision, reasoning, multimodal interaction, and typed decisions, built on a shared foundation.
    </box>
