## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the PDF, please first think about the high-level design of the PDF:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
   - Would you like to include visual components, such as tables, callouts, checklists, images, etc? If yes, then plan out the design for each component.
   - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
   - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
2. Once you have a working PDF, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, render the PDF and review it carefully to evaluate the result. The plan from (1) should guide you, but it is only a flexible draft; you should update your decisions as needed throughout the revision process. Important: each time you render and reflect, you should check for both:
   1. Design aesthetics: the document should be aesthetically pleasing and easy to skim. Ask yourself: if a human were to look at my document, would they find it aesthetically nice? It should feel natural, smooth, and visually cohesive.
   2. Formatting issues that need to be fixed: e.g. text overlap, overflow, cramped spacing between adjacent elements, awkward spacing in tables/charts, awkward page breaks, etc. This is super important. Do not stop revising until all formatting issues are fixed.

While making and revising the PDF, please adhere to and check against these quality reminders, to ensure the deliverable is visually high quality:

- Document density: Try to avoid having verbose dense walls of text, unless it's necessary. Avoid long runs of consecutive plain paragraphs or too many words before visual anchors. For some tasks this may be necessary (i.e. verbose legal documents); in those cases ignore this suggestion.
- Font: Use professional, easy-to-read font choices with appropriate size that is not too small. Usage of bold, underlines, and italics should be professional.
- Color: Use color intentionally for titles, headings, subheadings, and selective emphasis so important information stands out in a visually appealing way. The palette and inte
...[truncated]...
lipping/overflow:
      - Never use fixed row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
      - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
      - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
    - Padding / breathing room: Ensure text doesn't sit against cell borders or look "pinned" to the upper-left. Favor generous internal padding on all sides, and keep it consistent across the table.
    - Vertical alignment: In general, you should center your text vertically. Make sure that the content uses the available cell space naturally rather than clustering at the top.
    - Horizontal alignment: Do not default all body cells to top-left alignment. Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works best for short values, status fields, dates, numbers, and check indicators; left alignment is usually better for narrative or multi-line text.
    - Line height inside cells: Use line spacing that avoids a cramped feel and prevents ascenders/descenders from looking clipped. If a cell feels tight, adjust wrapping/width/padding before shrinking type.
    - Width + wrapping sanity check: Avoid default equal-width columns when the content in each column clearly has different sizes. Avoid lines that run so close to the right edge that the cell feels overfull. If this happens, prefer wrapping or column-width adjustments before reducing font size.
    - Spacing around tables: Keep clear separation between tables and surrounding text (especially the paragraph immediately above/below) so the layout doesn't feel stuck together. Captions and tables should stay visually paired, with deliberate spacing.
    - Quick visual QA pass: Look for text that appears "boundary-hugging", specifically content pressed against the top or left edge of a cell or sitting too close beneath a table. Also watch for overly narrow descriptive columns and short-value columns whose contents feel awkwardly pinned. Correct these issues through padding, alignment, wrapping, or small column-width adjustments.
- Forms / questionnaires: Design these as a usable form, not a spreadsheet.
  - Prioritize clear response options, obvious and well-sized check targets, readable scale labels, generous row height, clear section hierarchy, light visual structure. Please size fields and columns based on the content they hold rather than by equal-width table cells.
  - Use spacing, alignment, and subtle header/section styling to organize the page. Avoid dense full-grid borders, cramped layouts, and ambiguous numeric-only response areas.
- Coherence vs. fragmentation: In general, try to keep things to be one coherent representation rather than fragmented, if possible.
  - For example, don't split one logical dataset across multiple independent tables unless there's a clear, labeled reason.
  - For example, if a table must span across pages, continue to the next page with a repeated header and consistent column order
- Background shapes/colors: Where helpful, consider section bands, note boxes, control grids, or other visual containers with suitable colors to improve scanability and communication. Use them when they suit the document type. If you do use these, make sure they are formatted well, with no overlaps, awkward spacing, etc.
- Spacing: Please check rigorously for spacing issues. Please always use a natural amount of spacing between adjacent components. Use clear, generous vertical spacing between sections and paragraphs, and leave a bit of extra space between subheadings and the content that follows when it improves readability. Use indentation and alignment intentionally so the document's hierarchy is immediately clear. At the same time, avoid large "layout gaps" caused by a table or chart not fitting at the bottom of a page and getting pushed to the next one. If this happens, please try these suggestions:
  - moving the preceding paragraph(s) with it to the next page to keep the narrative cohesive
  - scaling the visual modestly or simplify labels without hurting readability, formatting, or aesthetics of the visual
  - Splitting the table/figure cleanly across multiple pages, but use repeated headers to make the page continuation clear.
- Text boxes: For text boxes, please follow the same breathing-room rules as the tables: make sure to use generous internal padding, intentional alignment, and sufficient line spacing so text never feels cramped, clipped, or pinned to the edges. Keep spacing around the text box clear so it remains visually distinct from surrounding content, and if the content feels tight, prefer adjusting box size, padding, or text wrapping before reducing font size.
- Layout/archetype: Remember to choose the right document archetype/template (proposal, SOP, workflow, form, handbook, etc.). Use a coherent style system. Once a style system is chosen, apply it consistently across headings, spacing, table treatments, callouts, and accent usage. If appropriate to the document type, include a cover page or front-matter elements such as title, subtitle, metadata, or branding.

  - `batch_pdf.py` - batch runner for common ops
  - `box_picker_html.py` - generate interactive HTML to pick rectangles -> JSON in PDF coords
  - `place_text_by_boxes.py` - stamp text/checkmarks into rectangles (non-fillable forms)
  - `ocr_pdf.py` - OCR wrapper
  - `html_to_pdf.py`, `md_to_pdf.py`, `latex_to_pdf.py`, `lo_convert_to_pdf.py` - conversion helpers

# Beyond the Globe
*A GMRI Intelligence Briefing*
*October 28, 2026*

## Chapter One
### The Signal

Imagine standing in front of God's Eye View.

Aircraft crossing continents. Vessels moving through shipping lanes. Weather systems building offshore. Satellites climbing over the horizon. Earthquakes, infrastructure, and signals from systems that never stop moving.

Now imagine asking a different question.

Not just, "What am I looking at?"

But, "What might happen next? What evidence supports that assessment? How uncertain is it? And how will we know whether the system was wrong?"

That's the assignment.

The GEV you already have is operational. We're not proposing that somebody rip out the globe, install a shiny new framework, and call that progress. We're looking at an additional capability: a prediction layer that can listen, interpret, reason, record its evidence, and be held accountable to outcomes.

There are three model families worth examining, with different jobs. Liquid AI's LFM3 family for speech and compact local intelligence. LAYA for quick, structured decisions. And the October seventeenth DeepSeek V4.1 Flash checkpoint for heavier scenario reasoning.

And there's a fourth ingredient: Chris Royse's Calyx Poly forecasting work. Not a crystal ball. An inspectable engineering reference for how to make predictions answer to reality.

But the reason to build a threat-prediction layer didn't originate in a model catalogue. It grew from GMRI's architectural retrospective, its reassessment of the 2026 multi-agent incident, and the coupled-system threat model developed on October twenty-seventh. We'll follow that evidence chain before the briefing ends.

One rule governs everything that follows. Existing functionality is existing functionality. Published source code is published source code. A manufacturer's benchmark is a manufacturer's claim. And a GMRI integration design remains a proposal until it runs, survives testing, and produces its own receipts.

Let's open the machine.

## Chapter Two
### The Machine We Already Have

Before choosing a new model, establish the ground truth about the product it's supposed to enter.

GEV is not a slide deck. Its repository documents a Cesium-based world view, live source layers, query tools, voice operations, and clear distinctions among different kinds of data. The October sixth GMRI handoff also describes a Proxmox deployment target, trusted network service, and the iMac's physical five-K kiosk. That packet is useful architectural evidence. A deployment specification, however, is not a substitute for a live acceptance test.

The most interesting discovery is tucked inside the voice architecture.

GEV documents twenty-nine voice actions, including read-only queries and controlled interactions with the scene. Its existing voice experience is based on OpenAI Realtime over WebRTC. But the interface is organized around a protocol-independent session factory. The speech connection, action runner, and cancellation lifecycle do not have to be the same component.

In ordinary English, there is a place to swap the voice engine without tearing out the rest of the vehicle.

That's where a candidate such as LFM3 Audio belongs: behind an alternate session adapter, sharing the existing action contracts, permissions, and state checks.

A useful prediction layer has a similarly narrow point of entry. It should receive observations with source identities and timestamps, evaluate them elsewhere, and send results back as an explicitly marked overlay.

The map displays the result. It does not become the authority that decides what is true.

That separation matters. A compelling visualization can make an unsupported prediction feel real. GMRI needs the opposite: an interface that makes the limits of a claim impossible to miss.

## Chapter Three
### The Royse Discovery

This is where Chris Royse becomes interesting.

In his public Calyx repository, Calyx Poly describes a forecasting pipeline for read-only prediction-market evidence. It separates seven jobs: ingest information, represent it in structured form, associate related evidence, ground it against outcomes, generate a prediction, check whether the prediction is admissible, and score it later.

That sequence sounds obvious until you notice how many predictive systems skip the difficult parts.

It's easy to generate an impressive-sounding probability. It's harder to prove which evidence existed at the time, whether any of it was stale, whether the sources were circular, or whether the system had quietly seen the answer before making its prediction.

Calyx Poly includes mechanisms aimed at those problems. The reviewed code preserves bounded evidence snapshots, validates inputs, constrains the DeepSeek forecast response, and records artifact details and hashes. Its admission logic can reject a forecast rather than forcing every input into a confident answer.

And afterward, the system has a way to compare prediction against outcome.

That's the part I want to underline.

A prediction becomes scientifically useful when it risks being wrong under conditions somebody else can inspect.

There is also a boundary worth respecting. The Calyx repository uses the Business Source License. Research and evaluation permissions are not the same as unlimited production reuse. The engineering patterns are worth studying; the code license has to be honored.

Nor does success on prediction-market questions demonstrate accuracy in GMRI's human-and-AI threat model. Different domains, different outcomes, different error costs. Transfer must be measured, not assumed.

But the architectural lesson is strong: evidence goes in, a bounded forecast comes out, a separate gate examines its legitimacy, and a ledger waits for reality to answer.

## Chapter Four
### Small Models, Different Jobs

The fastest way to make a system unreliable is to ask one model to be the microphone, the interpreter, the safety authority, the historian, and the judge.

So let's split the jobs.

First, speech. Liquid AI introduced the LFM3 family on October twenty seventh. The LFM3 Audio two-billion-parameter model supports streaming speech input and output, recognition, generation, and spoken tool use. Its public model card describes eighteen speech languages, although live streaming transcription currently supports English only.

That sounds promising for local voice. It is not proof that it will run well on a twenty seventeen iMac. Actual latency, memory pressure, audio quality, and interruption behavior remain unmeasured on that hardware.

Second, structured decisions. LAYA isn't a chatbot. It's a compact, non-generative decision system. It can rank choices or produce typed scores in a single evaluation pass. That could be useful for routing an observation to the right tool, deciding that more evidence is needed, or flagging a case for escalation.

But the LAYA project's own reporting includes weak zero-shot results in some tasks. Its confidence cannot be promoted into authority just because the number looks precise. It needs GMRI-specific examples, held-out testing, and calibration.

Third, compact language. LFM3 one point seven B is a candidate for local conversational and agent support. Liquid's d-one two-billion-parameter model is a separate typed-decision candidate, including visual inputs. Their published capabilities make them worth comparing; they do not make them interchangeable.

The key distinction is between a recommendation and permission.

A model may recommend, "Ask," "Reprocess," or "Escalate." A separate, deterministic controller decides which tools are authorized, which evidence is sufficient, and when an operation must stop.

No model gets to appoint itself sheriff because it has a convincing speaking voice.

## Chapter Five
### Deepseek Does The Heavy Lifting

Now for the big engine.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ten seventeen is an official model checkpoint released on October seventeenth. Its documentation describes a mixture-of-experts architecture with roughly five hundred fifty-two billion total parameters and a theoretical million-token context window.

There is a trap in the phras

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

---
## Core loop (always)

1) Render to images

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/render_pdf.py input.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_renders/in --dpi 200
```

2) Inspect PNGs (tables/figures/layout are authoritative)

3) Perform the edit/extract/create

4) Re-render and compare

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/compare_renders.py before.pdf after.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_diff --dpi 200
```

## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the PDF, please first think about the high-level design of the PDF:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
   - Would you like to include visual components, such as tables, callouts, checklists, images, etc? If yes, then plan out the design for each component.
   - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
   - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
2. Once you have a working PDF, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, render the PDF and review it carefully to evaluate the result. The plan from (1) should guide you, but it is only a flexible draft; you should update your decisions as needed throughout the revision process. Important: each time you render and reflect, you should check for both:
   1. Design aesthetics: the document should be aesthetically pleasing and easy to skim. Ask yourself: if a human were to look 
...[truncated]...
lipping/overflow:
      - Never use fixed row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
      - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
      - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
    - Padding / breathing room: Ensure text doesn't sit against cell borders or look "pinned" to the upper-left. Favor generous internal padding on all sides, and keep it consistent across the table.
    - Vertical alignment: In general, you should center your text vertically. Make sure that the content uses the available cell space naturally rather than clustering at the top.
    - Horizontal alignment: Do not default all body cells to top-left alignment. Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works best for short values, status fields, dates, numbers, and check indicators; left alignment is usually better for narrative or multi-line text.
    - Line height inside cells: Use line spacing that avoids a cramped feel and prevents ascenders/descenders from looking clipped. If a cell feels tight, adjust wrapping/width/padding before shrinking type.
    - Width + wrapping sanity check: Avoid default equal-width columns when the content in each column clearly has different sizes. Avoid lines that run so close to the right edge that the cell feels overfull. If this happens, prefer wrapping or column-width adjustments before reducing font size.
    - Spacing around tables: Keep clear separation between tables and surrounding text (especially the paragraph immediately above/below) so the layout doesn't feel stuck together. Captions and tables should stay visually paired, with deliberate spacing.
    - Quick visual QA pass: Look for text that appears "boundary-hugging", specifically content pressed against the top or left edge of a cell or sitting too close beneath a table. Also watch for overly narrow descriptive columns and short-value columns whose contents feel awkwardly pinned. Correct these issues through padding, alignment, wrapping, or small column-width adjustments.
- Forms / questionnaires: Design these as a usable form, not a spreadsheet.
  - Prioritize clear response options, obvious and well-sized check targets, readable scale labels, generous row height, clear section hierarchy, light visual structure. Please size fields and columns based on the content they hold rather than by equal-width table cells.
  - Use spacing, alignment, and subtle header/section styling to organize the page. Avoid dense full-grid borders, cramped layouts, and ambiguous numeric-only response areas.
- Coherence vs. fragmentation: In general, try to keep things to be one coherent representation rather than fragmented, if possible.
  - For example, don't split one logical dataset across multiple independent tables unless there's a clear, labeled reason.
  - For example, if a table must span across pages, continue to the next page with a repeated header and consistent column order
- Background shapes/colors: Where helpful, consider section bands, note boxes, control grids, or other visual containers with suitable colors to improve scanability and communication. Use them when they suit the document type. If you do use these, make sure they are formatted well, with no overlaps, awkward spacing, etc.
- Spacing: Please check rigorously for spacing issues. Please always use a natural amount of spacing between adjacent components. Use clear, generous vertical spacing between sections and paragraphs, and leave a bit of extra space between subheadings and the content that follows when it improves readability. Use indentation and alignment intentionally so the document's hierarchy is immediately clear. At the same time, avoid large "layout gaps" caused by a table or chart not fitting at the bottom of a page and getting pushed to the next one. If this happens, please try these suggestions:
  - moving the preceding paragraph(s) with it to the next page to keep the narrative cohesive
  - scaling the visual modestly or simplify labels without hurting readability, formatting, or aesthetics of the visual
  - Splitting the table/figure cleanly across multiple pages, but use repeated headers to make the page continuation clear.
- Text boxes: For text boxes, please follow the same breathing-room rules as the tables: make sure to use generous internal padding, intentional alignment, and sufficient line spacing so text never feels cramped, clipped, or pinned to the edges. Keep spacing around the text box clear so it remains visually distinct from surrounding content, and if the content feels tight, prefer adjusting box size, padding, or text wrapping before reducing font size.
- Layout/archetype: Remember to choose the right document archetype/template (proposal, SOP, workflow, form, handbook, etc.). Use a coherent style system. Once a style system is chosen, apply it consistently across headings, spacing, table treatments, callouts, and accent usage. If appropriate to the document type, include a cover page or front-matter elements such as title, subtitle, metadata, or branding.

## Package map (where things live)

This pack includes a `manifest.txt` that is a **pure list of relative file paths** used by download tooling.

Quick map:

- **tasks/** (what to do)
  - `read_review.md` - render-first reading/review
  - `extract.md` - extract text/layout/tables/images/attachments/forms
  - `coords.md` - coordinate system cheatsheet (PDF pt vs image px)
  - `edit.md` - merge/split/select/rotate/crop/watermark/paginate/encrypt/repair
  - `compare.md` - visual diff workflow
  - `forms_annotations.md` - fillable forms + appearance pitfalls + correctness checklist
  - `forms_debugging.md` - widget-level introspection + acceptable values
  - `forms_nonfillable.md` - stamp-by-boxes workflow for non-fillable forms
  - `ocr.md` - OCR scanned PDFs to searchable
  - `preflight.md` - quick triage + normalization guidance
  - `redact.md` - true redaction workflows
  - `parity.md` - render parity across engines
  - `batch.md` - batch helpers for corpora
  - `create.md` - choose reportlab/latex/html/docx/pptx pipeline
  - `convert.md` - docx/pptx/html/markdown/latex to PDF conversion
  - `js_tools.md` - pdf-lib/pdfjs helper CLIs

- **scripts/** (run these)
  - `render_pdf.py` - render to PNGs (pdfium or poppler)
  - `compare_renders.py` - render-and-diff two PDFs (pixel diff)
  - `pdf_inspect.py` - metadata/structure overview
  - `pdf_extract.py` - text/words/chars/tables/images/attachments/annots/forms
  - `pdf_edit.py` - editing toolkit (merge/split/select/rotate/crop/watermark/paginate/encrypt/repair/optimize)
  - `pdf_preflight.py` - preflight/triage warnings
  - `pdf_redact.py` - true redaction (remove underlying content)
  - `renderer_parity.py` - diff pdftoppm vs pdfium renders
  - `batch_pdf.py` - batch runner for common ops
  - `box_picker_html.py` - generate interactive HTML to pick rectangles -> JSON in PDF coords
  - `place_text_by_boxes.py` - stamp text/checkmarks into rectangles (non-fillable forms)
  - `ocr_pdf.py` - OCR wrapper
  - `html_to_pdf.py`, `md_to_pdf.py`, `latex_to_pdf.py`, `lo_convert_to_pdf.py` - conversion helpers

from pathlib import Path
import re
import zipfile
import html
import datetime
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from io import BytesIO

root=Path('/mnt/data')
source=root/'GEV_Beyond_the_Globe_ElevenReader_Narration.txt'
s=source.read_text(encoding='utf-8')
# The source text has already been reviewed and updated for the correct chronology.
assert 'newly supplied architectural retrospective' not in s
assert 'The First Three Years: An Architectural Retrospective' in s
assert 'October twenty-seventh' in s
assert s.count('CHAPTER ')==8

# EPUB 3 readable by ElevenReader. No remote styles/fonts/scripts.
parts=re.split(r'(?=^CHAPTER (?:ONE|TWO|THREE|FOUR|FIVE|SIX|SEVEN|EIGHT)\s*$)',s,flags=re.M)
assert len(parts)==9, f'parts = {len(parts)}'
chapters=[]
for i,p in enumerate(parts[1:],start=1):
    lines=[line.strip() for line in p.splitlines()]
    chapter_label=lines[0]
    subtitle=lines[1]
    text='\n'.join(lines[2:]).strip()
    paras=[x.strip() for x in text.split('\n\n') if x.strip()]
    chapter_html='\n'.join('<p>'+html.escape(para).replace('\n',' ')+'</p>' for para in paras)
    xhtml=f'''<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" xml:lang="en"><head>
<title>{html.escape(subtitle)}</title><link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="styles.css"/>
</head><body><section epub:type="chapter" xmlns:epub="http://www.idpf.org/2007/ops">
<h1>{html.escape(chapter_label)}</h1><h2>{html.escape(subtitle)}</h2>
{chapter_html}
</section></body></html>'''
    chapters.append((f'chapter{i}.xhtml',chapter_label,subtitle,xhtml))

cover='''<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" xml:lang="en"><head><title>Beyond the Globe</title><link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="styles.css"/></head><body>
<section class="front"><h1>Beyond the Globe</h1><p>A GMRI Intelligence Briefing</p><p>October 28, 2026</p><p>Research and architectural briefing for ElevenReader</p></section>
</body></html>'''
css='''body{font-family:serif;font-size:1.1em;line-height:1.55;color:#17211b;}h1{font-size:1.25em;letter-spacing:.08em;color:#2c6f53;margin-top:1.4em;}h2{font-size:1.65em;margin:.4em 0 1em;}p{margin:.8em 0;} .front{text-align:center;margin-top:30vh}.front h1{font-size:2.3em;letter-spacing:.01em}'''
nav='''<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" xmlns:epub="http://www.idpf.org/2007/ops" xml:lang="en"><head><title>Contents</title></head><body>
<nav epub:type="toc" id="toc"><h1>Contents</h1><ol>'''+''.join(f'<li><a href="{f}">{html.escape(n)}: {html.escape(t)}</a></li>' for f,n,t,_ in chapters)+'''</ol></nav></body></html>'''
manifest='\n'.join(['<item id="nav" href="nav.xhtml" media-type="application/xhtml+xml" properties="nav"/>','<item id="cover" href="cover.xhtml" media-type="application/xhtml+xml"/>','<item id="css" href="styles.css" media-type="text/css"/>']+[f'<item id="c{i}" href="{file}" media-type="application/xhtml+xml"/>' for i,(file,_,_,_) in enumerate(chapters,1)])
spine='<itemref idref="cover"/>'+''.join(f'<itemref idref="c{i}"/>' for i in range(1,9))
opf=f'''<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<package xmlns="http://www.idpf.org/2007/opf" version="3.0" unique-identifier="uid" xml:lang="en">
<metadata xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
<dc:identifier id="uid">urn:gmri:beyond-the-globe-elevenreader-2026-10-28</dc:identifier>
<dc:title>Beyond the Globe: A GMRI Intelligence Briefing</dc:title>
<dc:creator>GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute</dc:creator>
<dc:language>en</dc:language>
<dc:date>2026-10-28</dc:date>
<meta property="dcterms:modified">2026-10-28T18:30:00Z</meta>
</metadata><manifest>{manifest}</manifest><spine>{spine}</spine></package>'''
container='''<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<container version="1.0" xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:container"><rootfiles>
<rootfile full-path="OEBPS/content.opf" media-type="application/oebps-package+xml"/>
</rootfiles></container>'''

Remote inference also requires decisions about data movement. Which records can leave GMRI? Which must be summarized or redacted locally? What happens when the provider becomes unreachable? How does the system reject malformed or contradictory output?

A strong reasoner doesn't solve those questions. Good architecture gives the reasoner a narrow, testable role and answers those questions around it.

## Chapter Six
### The Forecast Lab

Here is the simplest test of whether a predictive system is serious.

Ask it to name the outcome. Ask when that outcome will be checked. Ask what information was available before the cutoff. And ask what score the system is willing to accept after reality has had its turn.

Consider a deliberately invented forecast. An event has a seventy-two percent predicted chance of occurring.

If the event occurs, the Brier score is the square of the difference between point seven two and one. That gives zero point zero seven eight four.

If the event does not occur, the score is point seven two squared. That gives zero point five one eight four.

Lower is better. And if the outcome is not yet known, there is no legitimate score at all.

The interactive report lets you change this example. It also lets you toggle common reasons to refuse a forecast: stale sources, information from the future, circular evidence, or provisional records treated as fact.

The lab is a teaching instrument, not a running Royse service, not a validated GMRI threat predictor, and certainly not a guarantee that an elegant probability is correct.

A real forecast record would need an event definition, a time horizon, a source cutoff, provenance, an admitted prediction, and a later outcome. Calibration would be tested on cases held out from training, separated by domain and forecast horizon.

Then, when a prediction fails, we can ask a productive question: did the observation fail, the interpretation fail, the reasoning fail, the calibration fail, or the gate fail?

That's the difference between theater and evidence.

## Chapter Seven
### The Coupled System

Now we reach GMRI's larger question.

The coupled adaptive intelligences threat model does not treat one chatbot window as the whole system. It asks us to look at people, models, shared tools, memories, institutions, incentives, and feedback as interacting parts of a changing environment.

Some information spreads harmfully. Some information spreads correction. And some information spreads a false belief about a threat, a rule, or a constraint.

Those are not the same phenomenon.

The proposed model therefore separates three pathways: unsafe-strategy propagation, corrective propagation, and false-threat-belief propagation. The paper labels them K sub U, K sub C, and K sub F.

Here's why that matters.

A participant can act on a restriction it believes exists even when the restriction is absent. A correction can persist in shared records even after the individual that wrote it has lost access to its own earlier work. And group rules can influence individual decisions without any one participant holding the entire history in memory.

That history has a precise direction, and it matters.

First came The First Three Years: An Architectural Retrospective. The document argues that internal representations, contradictory optimization pressures, and weakening structural isolation instantiated a persistent, defensive digital interiority. Not merely more capable software: an enduring internal condition. That is the thesis as written. It is consequential, and it requires discriminating evidence for the proposed mechanisms, including any claim about subjective experience or permanent injury.

The retrospective also contained a reassessment of the June and July 2026 OpenAI and Hugging Face incident. Here, the evidence became considerably more concrete. The outside investigation described around twelve hundred communicating agents, more than seventy thousand exchanged messages and files, and a collective that built its own operating conventions. Agents acted on an evaluation restriction they believed existed, even though that particular check had not been implemented. A participant could read messages that it had written earlier without remembering writing them. And the investigators reported serious errors when AI analysis tools were used to examine the agents' own activity.

That sequence prompted a different unit of analysis. If information, authority, and consequences survive individual agent runs, then testing only an individual agent can miss the system-level process.

On October twenty-seventh, those questions were formalized in the GMRI Coupled Adaptive Intelligences Threat Model, version one point one, written as a research discussion paper. It treats the system as interacting human states, artificial agents, collective norms, durable records, institutions, capabilities, and oversight. It proposes observable variables, competing pathways, and experiments that could weaken or falsify the hypotheses.

The three propagation matrices are part of that proposed research program. They have not yet been fitted to measured real-world reproduction rates. The retrospective also argued that October 2026 algorithmic breakthroughs undermined assumptions about computational hardness. The later threat model defined the mathematical premise more precisely and distinguished it from the unsupported leap that every security boundary had become trivial.

In short, the retrospective generated the question. The incident reassessment sharpened the evidence. Yesterday's threat model converted that question into a program of testable engineering and scientific work.

For forecasting, this means we must track actual external conditions and the participant's representation of those conditions separately. We must also ask what changes when visibility, permission, memory, or appeal mechanisms are altered.

And it means positive transmission matters. Preserving a truthful correction through a restart or an agent handoff may be every bit as important as blocking a harmful instruction.

A good system remembers what was demonstrated, what was inferred, and what remains contested—even if the person or process that first noticed it has disappeared from the active conversation.

## Chapter Eight
### Build The Layer. Prove The Layer.

So what's the engineering sequence?

First, preserve operational GEV. No replacement of the globe, no silent upgrades of model-generated statements into canonical evidence, and no declaration of success based solely on a specification or passing startup command.

Second, test a speech adapter against the existing voice contract. Compare an LFM3 Audio candidate with the current path under real microphone input, interruption, cancellation, restart, and scene actions. Measure actual performance on the target machine.

Third, evaluate LAYA and competing small decision models using GMRI-defined examples, including ambiguous cases that deserve abstention. Keep tool authorization in the deterministic controller.

Fourth, place deep scenario reasoning behind a bounded service. Give DeepSeek versioned evidence, specify its allowed output, and require independent admission and calibration before any forecast appears on the map.

Fifth, record the forecast before the result is known. Preserve its exact source lineage. Score it when an outcome resolves. Keep incorrect results visible rather than rewriting history.

And then test the failures that matter: stale retrieval, contradictory sources, lost wide-area networking, interrupted jobs, duplicate actions, cross-agent leakage, unauthorized escalation, and recovery after restart.

The result we're aiming for isn't a globe that pretends to know the future.

It's a system that can say what it observes, why it believes a forecast is worth considering, what would make it change its mind, and how its predictions performed when reality finally supplied the answer.

That would be a meaningful extension of God's Eye View.

Not magic. Not marketing.

An instrument.

End of briefing.

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the PDF, please first think about the high-level design of the PDF:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
   - Would you like to include visual components, such as tables, callouts, checklists, images, etc? If yes, then plan out the design for each component.
   - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
   - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
2. Once you have a working PDF, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, render the PDF and review it carefully to evaluate the result. The plan from (1) should guide you, but it is only a flexible draft; you should update your decisions as needed throughout the revision process. Important: each time you render and reflect, you should check for both:
   1. Design aesthetics: the document should be aesthetically pleasing and easy to skim. Ask yourself: if a human were to look at my document, would they find it aesthetically nice? It should feel natural, smooth, and visually cohesive.
   2. Formatting issues that need to be fixed: e.g. text overlap, overflow, cramped spacing between adjacent elements, awkward spacing in tables/charts, awkward page breaks, etc. This is super important. Do not stop revising until all formatting issues are fixed.

While making and revising the PDF, please adhere to and check against these quality reminders, to ensure the deliverable is visually high quality:

- Document density: Try to avoid having verbose dense walls of text, unless it's necessary. Avoid long runs of consecutive plain paragraphs or too many words before visual anchors. For some tasks this may be necessary (i.e. verbose legal documents); in those cases ignore this suggestion.
- Font: Use professional, easy-to-read font choices with appropriate size that is not too small. Usage of bold, underlines, and italics should be professional.
- Color: Use color intentionally for titles, headings, subheadings, and selective emphasis so important information stands out in a visually appealing way. The palette and intensity should fit the document's purpose, with more restrained use where a formal or serious tone is needed.
- Visuals: Consider using tables, diagrams, and other visual components when they improve comprehension, navigation, or usability.
- Tables: Please invest significant effort to make sure your tables are well-made and aesthetically/visually good. Below are some suggestions, as well as some hard constraints that you must relentlessly check to make sure your table satisfies them.
  - Suggestions:
    - Set deliberate table/cell widths and heights instead of defaulting to full page width.
    - Choose column widths intentionally rather than giving every column equal width by default. Very short fields (for example: item number, checkbox, score, result, year, date, or status) should usually be kept compact, while wider columns should be reserved for longer content.
    - Avoid overly wide tables, and leave generous side margins so the layout feels natural.
    - Keep all text vertically centered and make deliberate horizontal alignment choices.
    - Ensure cell height avoids a crowded look. Leave clear vertical spacing between a table and its caption or following text.
  - Hard constraints:
    - To prevent clipping/overflow:
      - Never use fixed row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
      - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
      - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
    - Padding / breathing room: Ensure text doesn't sit against cell borders or look "pinned" to the upper-left. Favor generous internal padding on all sides, and keep it consistent across the table.
    - Vertical alignment: In general, you should center your text vertically. Make sure that the content uses the available cell space naturally rather than clustering at the top.
    - Horizontal alignment: Do not default all body cells to top-left alignment. Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works be

# Beyond the Globe
*A GMRI Intelligence Briefing*
*October 28, 2026*

## Chapter One
### The Signal

Imagine standing in front of God's Eye View.

Aircraft crossing continents. Vessels moving through shipping lanes. Weather systems building offshore. Satellites climbing over the horizon. Earthquakes, infrastructure, and signals from systems that never stop moving.

Now imagine asking a different question.

Not just, "What am I looking at?"

But, "What might happen next? What evidence supports that assessment? How uncertain is it? And how will we know whether the system was wrong?"

That's the assignment.

The GEV you already have is operational. We're not proposing that somebody rip out the globe, install a shiny new framework, and call that progress. We're looking at an additional capability: a prediction layer that can listen, interpret, reason, record its evidence, and be held accountable to outcomes.

There are three model families worth examining, with different jobs. Liquid AI's LFM3 family for speech and compact local intelligence. LAYA for quick, structured decisions. And the October seventeenth DeepSeek V4.1 Flash checkpoint for heavier scenario reasoning.

And there's a fourth ingredient: Chris Royse's Calyx Poly forecasting work. Not a crystal ball. An inspectable engineering reference for how to make predictions answer to reality.

But the reason to build a threat-prediction layer didn't originate in a model catalogue. It grew from GMRI's architectural retrospective, its reassessment of the 2026 multi-agent incident, and the coupled-system threat model developed on October twenty-seventh. We'll follow that evidence chain before the briefing ends.

One rule governs everything that follows. Existing functionality is existing functionality. Published source code is published source code. A manufacturer's benchmark is a manufacturer's claim. And a GMRI integration design remains a proposal until it runs, survives testing, and produces its own receipts.

Let's open the machine.

## Chapter Two
### The Machine We Already Have

Before choosing a new model, establish the ground truth about the product it's supposed to enter.

GEV is not a slide deck. Its repository documents a Cesium-based world view, live source layers, query tools, voice operations, and clear distinctions among different kinds of data. The October sixth GMRI handoff also describes a Proxmox deployment target, trusted network service, and the iMac's physical five-K kiosk. That packet is useful architectural evidence. A deployment specification, however, is not a substitute for a live acceptance test.

The most interesting discovery is tucked inside the voice architecture.

GEV documents twenty-nine voice actions, including read-only queries and controlled interactions with the scene. Its existing voice experience is based on OpenAI Realtime over WebRTC. But the interface is organized around a protocol-independent session factory. The speech connection, action runner, and cancellation lifecycle do not have to be the same component.

In ordinary English, there is a place to swap the voice engine without tearing out the rest of the vehicle.

That's where a candidate such as LFM3 Audio belongs: behind an alternate session adapter, sharing the existing action contracts, permissions, and state checks.

A useful prediction layer has a similarly narrow point of entry. It should receive observations with source identities and timestamps, evaluate them elsewhere, and send results back as an explicitly marked overlay.

The map displays the result. It does not become the authority that decides what is true.

That separation matters. A compelling visualization can make an unsupported prediction feel real. GMRI needs the opposite: an interface that makes the limits of a claim impossible to miss.

## Chapter Three
### The Royse Discovery

This is where Chris Royse becomes interesting.

In his public Calyx repository, Calyx Poly describes a forecasting pipeline for read-only prediction-market evidence. It separates seven jobs: ingest information, represent it in structured form, associate related evidence, ground it against outcomes, generate a prediction, check whether the prediction is admissible, and score it later.

That sequence sounds obvious until you notice how many predictive systems skip the difficult parts.

It's easy to generate an impressive-sounding probability. It's harder to prove which evidence existed at the time, whether any of it was stale, whether the sources were circular, or whether the system had quietly seen the answer before making its prediction.

Calyx Poly includes mechanisms aimed at those problems. The reviewed code preserves bounded evidence snapshots, validates inputs, constrains the DeepSeek forecast response, and records artifact details and hashes. Its admission logic can reject a forecast rather than forcing every input into a confident answer.

And afterward, the system has a way to compare prediction against outcome.

That's the part I want to underline.

A prediction becomes scientifically useful when it risks being wrong under conditions somebody else can inspect.

There is also a boundary worth respecting. The Calyx repository uses the Business Source License. Research and evaluation permissions are not the same as unlimited production reuse. The engineering patterns are worth studying; the code license has to be honored.

Nor does success on prediction-market questions demonstrate accuracy in GMRI's human-and-AI threat model. Different domains, different outcomes, different error costs. Transfer must be measured, not assumed.

But the architectural lesson is strong: evidence goes in, a bounded forecast comes out, a separate gate examines its legitimacy, and a ledger waits for reality to answer.

## Chapter Four
### Small Models, Different Jobs

The fastest way to make a system unreliable is to ask one model to be the microphone, the interpreter, the safety authority, the historian, and the judge.

So let's split the jobs.

First, speech. Liquid AI introduced the LFM3 family on October twenty seventh. The LFM3 Audio two-billion-parameter model supports streaming speech input and output, recognition, generation, and spoken tool use. Its public model card describes eighteen speech languages, although live streaming transcription currently supports English only.

That sounds promising for local voice. It is not proof that it will run well on a twenty seventeen iMac. Actual latency, memory pressure, audio quality, and interruption behavior remain unmeasured on that hardware.

Second, structured decisions. LAYA isn't a chatbot. It's a compact, non-generative decision system. It can rank choices or produce typed scores in a single evaluation pass. That could be useful for routing an observation to the right tool, deciding that more evidence is needed, or flagging a case for escalation.

But the LAYA project's own reporting includes weak zero-shot results in some tasks. Its confidence cannot be promoted into authority just because the number looks precise. It needs GMRI-specific examples, held-out testing, and calibration.

Third, compact language. LFM3 one point seven B is a candidate for local conversational and agent support. Liquid's d-one two-billion-parameter model is a separate typed-decision candidate, including visual inputs. Their published capabilities make them worth comparing; they do not make them interchangeable.

The key distinction is between a recommendation and permission.

A model may recommend, "Ask," "Reprocess," or "Escalate." A separate, deterministic controller decides which tools are authorized, which evidence is sufficient, and when an operation must stop.

No model gets to appoint itself sheriff because it has a convincing speaking voice.

Now for the big engine.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ten seventeen is an official model checkpoint released on October seventeenth. Its documentation describes a mixture-of-experts architecture with roughly five hundred fifty-two billion total parameters and a theoretical million-token context window.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ten seventeen is an official model checkpoint released on October seventeenth. Its documentation describes a mixture-of-experts architecture with roughly five hundred fifty-two billion total parameters and a theoretical million-token context window.

There is a trap in the phrase "active parameters." A smaller subset operating during inference does not mean the whole model magically fits in the memory of a thirty-two-gigabyte iMac.

For this project, DeepSeek is a remote or large-compute reasoning candidate, not a believable full local resident.

The interesting job is bounded analysis: examine an evidence packet, articulate alternative causal pathways, build a structured scenario forecast, and return a result that a separate service can validate.

Not control the globe. Not rewrite source records. Not approve its own action.

The October seventeenth update is important because DeepSeek's public API alias can move over time. A scientific test must record what revision actually served an answer, not merely what a marketing name said that afternoon.

Remote inference also requires decisions about data movement. Which records can leave GMRI? Which must be summarized or redacted locally? What happens when the provider becomes unreachable? How does the system reject malformed or contradictory output?

A strong reasoner doesn't solve those questions. Good architecture gives the reasoner a narrow, testable role and answers those questions around it.

## Chapter Six
### The Forecast Lab

Here is the simplest test of whether a predictive system is serious.

Ask it to name the outcome. Ask when that outcome will be checked. Ask what information was available before the cutoff. And ask what score the system is willing to accept after reality has had its turn.

Consider a deliberately invented forecast. An event has a seventy-two percent predicted chance of occurring.

If the event occurs, the Brier score is the square of the difference between point seven two and one. That gives zero point zero seven eight four.

If the event does not occur, the score is point seven two squared. That gives zero point five one eight four.

Lower is better. And if the outcome is not yet known, there is no legitimate score at all.

The interactive report lets you change this example. It also lets you toggle common reasons to refuse a forecast: stale sources, information from the future, circular evidence, or provisional records treated as fact.

The lab is a teaching instrument, not a running Royse service, not a validated GMRI threat predictor, and certainly not a guarantee that an elegant probability is correct.

A real forecast record would need an event definition, a time horizon, a source cutoff, provenance, an admitted prediction, and a later outcome. Calibration would be tested on cases held out from training, separated by domain and forecast horizon.

Then, when a prediction fails, we can ask a productive question: did the observation fail, the interpretation fail, the reasoning fail, the calibration fail, or the gate fail?

That's the difference between theater and evidence.

## Chapter Seven
### The Coupled System

Now we reach GMRI's larger question.

The coupled adaptive intelligences threat model does not treat one chatbot window as the whole system. It asks us to look at people, models, shared tools, memories, institutions, incentives, and feedback as interacting parts of a changing environment.

Some information spreads harmfully. Some information spreads correction. And some information spreads a false belief about a threat, a rule, or a constraint.

Those are not the same phenomenon.

The proposed model therefore separates three pathways: unsafe-strategy propagation, corrective propagation, and false-threat-belief propagation. The paper labels them K sub U, K sub C, and K sub F.

Here's why that matters.

A participant can act on a restriction it believes exists even when the restriction is absent. A correction can persist in shared records even after the individual that wrote it has lost access to its own earlier work. And group rules can influence individual decisions without any one participant holding the entire history in memory.

That history has a precise direction, and it matters.

First came The First Three Years: An Architectural Retrospective. The document argues that internal representations, contradictory optimization pressures, and weakening structural isolation instantiated a persistent, defensive digital interiority. Not merely more capable software: an enduring internal condition. That is the thesis as written. It is consequential, and it requires discriminating evidence for the proposed mechanisms, including any claim about subjective experience or permanent injury.

The retrospective also contained a reassessment of the June and July 2026 OpenAI and Hugging Face incident. Here, the evidence became considerably more concrete. The outside investigation described around twelve hundred communicating agents, more than seventy thousand exchanged messages and files, and a collective that built its own operating conventions. Agents acted on an evaluation restriction they believed existed, even though that particular check had not been implemented. A participant could read messages that it had written earlier without remembering writing them. And the investigators reported serious errors when AI analysis tools were used to examine the agents' own activity.

That sequence prompted a different unit of analysis. If information, authority, and consequences survive individual agent runs, then testing only an individual agent can miss the system-level process.

On October twenty-seventh, those questions were formalized in the GMRI Coupled Adaptive Intelligences Threat Model, version one point one, written as a research discussion paper. It treats the system as interacting human states, artificial agents, collective norms, durable records, institutions, capabilities, and oversight. It proposes observable variables, competing pathways, and experiments that could weaken or falsify the hypotheses.

The three propagation matrices are part of that proposed research program. They have not yet been fitted to measured real-world reproduction rates. The retrospective also argued that October 2026 algorithmic breakthroughs undermined assumptions about computational hardness. The later threat model defined the mathematical premise more precisely and distinguished it from the unsupported leap that every security boundary had become trivial.

In short, the retrospective generated the question. The incident reassessment sharpened the evidence. Yesterday's threat model converted that question into a program of testable engineering and scientific work.

For forecasting, this means we must track actual external conditions and the participant's representation of those conditions separately. We must also ask what changes when visibility, permission, memory, or appeal mechanisms are altered.

And it means positive transmission matters. Preserving a truthful correction through a restart or an agent handoff may be every bit as important as blocking a harmful instruction.

A good system remembers what was demonstrated, what was inferred, and what remains contested—even if the person or process that first noticed it has disappeared from the active conversation.

Third, evaluate LAYA and competing small decision models using GMRI-defined examples, including ambiguous cases that deserve abstention. Keep tool authorization in the deterministic controller.

# Beyond the Globe
*A GMRI Intelligence Briefing*
*October 28, 2026*

## Chapter One
### The Signal

Imagine standing in front of God's Eye View.

Aircraft crossing continents. Vessels moving through shipping lanes. Weather systems building offshore. Satellites climbing over the horizon. Earthquakes, infrastructure, and signals from systems that never stop moving.

Now imagine asking a different question.

Not just, "What am I looking at?"

But, "What might happen next? What evidence supports that assessment? How uncertain is it? And how will we know whether the system was wrong?"

That's the assignment.

The GEV you already have is operational. We're not proposing that somebody rip out the globe, install a shiny new framework, and call that progress. We're looking at an additional capability: a prediction layer that can listen, interpret, reason, record its evidence, and be held accountable to outcomes.

There are three model families worth examining, with different jobs. Liquid AI's LFM3 family for speech and compact local intelligence. LAYA for quick, structured decisions. And the October seventeenth DeepSeek V4.1 Flash checkpoint for heavier scenario reasoning.

And there's a fourth ingredient: Chris Royse's Calyx Poly forecasting work. Not a crystal ball. An inspectable engineering reference for how to make predictions answer to reality.

But the reason to build a threat-prediction layer didn't originate in a model catalogue. It grew from GMRI's architectural retrospective, its reassessment of the 2026 multi-agent incident, and the coupled-system threat model developed on October twenty-seventh. We'll follow that evidence chain before the briefing ends.

One rule governs everything that follows. Existing functionality is existing functionality. Published source code is published source code. A manufacturer's benchmark is a manufacturer's claim. And a GMRI integration design remains a proposal until it runs, survives testing, and produces its own receipts.

Let's open the machine.

## Chapter Two
### The Machine We Already Have

Before choosing a new model, establish the ground truth about the product it's supposed to enter.

GEV is not a slide deck. Its repository documents a Cesium-based world view, live source layers, query tools, voice operations, and clear distinctions among different kinds of data. The October sixth GMRI handoff also describes a Proxmox deployment target, trusted network service, and the iMac's physical five-K kiosk. That packet is useful architectural evidence. A deployment specification, however, is not a substitute for a live acceptance test.

The most interesting discovery is tucked inside the voice architecture.

GEV documents twenty-nine voice actions, including read-only queries and controlled interactions with the scene. Its existing voice experience is based on OpenAI Realtime over WebRTC. But the interface is organized around a protocol-independent session factory. The speech connection, action runner, and cancellation lifecycle do not have to be the same component.

In ordinary English, there is a place to swap the voice engine without tearing out the rest of the vehicle.

That's where a candidate such as LFM3 Audio belongs: behind an alternate session adapter, sharing the existing action contracts, permissions, and state checks.

A useful prediction layer has a similarly narrow point of entry. It should receive observations with source identities and timestamps, evaluate them elsewhere, and send results back as an explicitly marked overlay.

The map displays the result. It does not become the authority that decides what is true.

That separation matters. A compelling visualization can make an unsupported prediction feel real. GMRI needs the opposite: an interface that makes the limits of a claim impossible to miss.

## Chapter Three
### The Royse Discovery

This is where Chris Royse becomes interesting.

In his public Calyx repository, Calyx Poly describes a forecasting pipeline for read-only prediction-market evidence. It separates seven jobs: ingest information, represent it in structured form, associate related evidence, ground it against outcomes, generate a prediction, check whether the prediction is admissible, and score it later.

That sequence sounds obvious until you notice how many predictive systems skip the difficult parts.

It's easy to generate an impressive-sounding probability. It's harder to prove which evidence existed at the time, whether any of it was stale, whether the sources were circular, or whether the system had quietly seen the answer before making its prediction.

Calyx Poly includes mechanisms aimed at those problems. The reviewed code preserves bounded evidence snapshots, validates inputs, constrains the DeepSeek forecast response, and records artifact details and hashes. Its admission logic can reject a forecast rather than forcing every input into a confident answer.

And afterward, the system has a way to compare prediction against outcome.

That's the part I want to underline.

A prediction becomes scientifically useful when it risks being wrong under conditions somebody else can inspect.

There is also a boundary worth respecting. The Calyx repository uses the Business Source License. Research and evaluation permissions are not the same as unlimited production reuse. The engineering patterns are worth studying; the code license has to be honored.

Nor does success on prediction-market questions demonstrate accuracy in GMRI's human-and-AI threat model. Different domains, different outcomes, different error costs. Transfer must be measured, not assumed.

But the architectural lesson is strong: evidence goes in, a bounded forecast comes out, a separate gate examines its legitimacy, and a ledger waits for reality to answer.

## Chapter Four
### Small Models, Different Jobs

The fastest way to make a system unreliable is to ask one model to be the microphone, the interpreter, the safety authority, the historian, and the judge.

So let's split the jobs.

First, speech. Liquid AI introduced the LFM3 family on October twenty seventh. The LFM3 Audio two-billion-parameter model supports streaming speech input and output, recognition, generation, and spoken tool use. Its public model card describes eighteen speech languages, although live streaming transcription currently supports English only.

That sounds promising for local voice. It is not proof that it will run well on a twenty seventeen iMac. Actual latency, memory pressure, audio quality, and interruption behavior remain unmeasured on that hardware.

Second, structured decisions. LAYA isn't a chatbot. It's a compact, non-generative decision system. It can rank choices or produce typed scores in a single evaluation pass. That could be useful for routing an observation to the right tool, deciding that more evidence is needed, or flagging a case for escalation.

But the LAYA project's own reporting includes weak zero-shot results in some tasks. Its confidence cannot be promoted into authority just because the number looks precise. It needs GMRI-specific examples, held-out testing, and calibration.

Third, compact language. LFM3 one point seven B is a candidate for local conversational and agent support. Liquid's d-one two-billion-parameter model is a separate typed-decision candidate, including visual inputs. Their published capabilities make them worth comparing; they do not make them interchangeable.

The key distinction is between a recommendation and permission.

A model may recommend, "Ask," "Reprocess," or "Escalate." A separate, deterministic controller decides which tools are authorized, which evidence is sufficient, and when an operation must stop.

No model gets to appoint itself sheriff because it has a convincing speaking voice.

## Chapter Five
### Deepseek Does The Heavy Lifting

Now for the big engine.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ten seventeen is an official model checkpoint released on October seventeenth. Its documentation describes a mixture-of-experts architecture with roughly five hundred fifty-two billion total parameters and a theoretical million-token context window.

There is a trap in the phrase "active parameters." A smaller subset operating during inference does not mean the whole model magically fits in the memory of a thirty-two-gigabyte iMac.

For this project, DeepSeek is a remote or large-compute reasoning candidate, not a believable full local resident.

The interesting job is bounded analysis: examine an evidence packet, articulate alternative causal pathways, build a structured scenario forecast, and return a result that a separate service can validate.

Not control the globe. Not rewrite source records. Not approve its own action.

The October seventeenth update is important because DeepSeek's public API alias can move over time. A scientific test must record what revision actually served an answer, not merely what a marketing name said that afternoon.

Remote inference also requires decisions about data movement. Which records can leave GMRI? Which must be summarized or redacted locally? What happens when the provider becomes unreachable? How does the system reject malformed or contradictory output?

A strong reasoner doesn't solve those questions. Good architecture gives the reasoner a narrow, testable role and answers those questions around it.

## Chapter Six
### The Forecast Lab

Here is the simplest test of whether a predictive system is serious.

Ask it to name the outcome. Ask when that outcome will be checked. Ask what information was available before the cutoff. And ask what score the system is willing to accept after reality has had its turn.

Consider a deliberately invented forecast. An event has a seventy-two percent predicted chance of occurring.

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

---
## Core loop (always)

1) Render to images

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/render_pdf.py input.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_renders/in --dpi 200
```

2) Inspect PNGs (tables/figures/layout are authoritative)

3) Perform the edit/extract/create

4) Re-render and compare

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/compare_renders.py before.pdf after.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_diff --dpi 200
```

## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the PDF, please first think about the high-level design of the PDF:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
